For a long time African rulers negotiated with the Europeans as equals. The kings of Kongo exchanged envoys with Portugal and the pope, Njinga of Ndongo and Matamba alternated between war, diplomacy and alliances with the Dutch, and the Merina kings of Madagascar concluded treaties with Britain. Only in the 19th century did European pressure grow so strong that states such as Ethiopia under Tewodros II or the Zulu kingdom were drawn into open wars with Britain.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The great majority of people lived as farmers, herders or fishermen in villages led by kinship groups and elders. Millet, sorghum, yams and rice, and in East Africa also bananas, formed the basis of their diet; cattle were a sign of wealth and prestige, especially in the south and east. Because land was usually plentiful but labor scarce, power was measured above all by the number of people who followed a ruler or the head of a family.

Many societies had hereditary occupational groups such as smiths, weavers or griots, who served at the courts as singers and keepers of history. Slavery was widespread in numerous African states, but it often differed from the plantation slavery of the Americas: unfree people worked as farmers, soldiers, servants or even officials, and their descendants could be absorbed into the families of their masters. The Atlantic slave trade, however, intensified kidnapping and warfare and turned captives into a commodity on a previously unknown scale.

Women played a visible role in many African societies. Queen mothers such as the iyoba in Benin or the asantehemaa in Asante had their own courts and political influence, and female rulers such as Njinga or Ranavalona I governed in their own right. Market women dominated the markets of West Africa, in Dahomey female warriors formed a unit of their own, and the scholar Nana Asma'u organized education for women in the Sokoto Caliphate.

Cities such as Timbuktu, Djenné, Kano, Kilwa, Benin or Kumasi were densely populated centers with markets, palaces and places of worship. Travellers such as Ibn Battuta described the security, prosperity and strict order of Mali, and Portuguese visitors compared Benin with European cities. Here merchants from North Africa, Arabia and India met local traders, and mixed cultures such as that of the Swahili emerged.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: Alongside indigenous religions, which venerated ancestors, the forces of nature and a creator god, Christianity and Islam spread. Aksum and the kingdoms of Nubia became Christian as early as the 4th to 6th centuries, and the Ethiopian church developed a distinctive tradition with Ge'ez as its liturgical language, its own saints and the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela. Islam came to the Sahel through merchants from North Africa and to the east coast through the seafaring traders of the Indian Ocean, and was at first adopted mainly by rulers and traders.

Writing and scholarship were far more widespread than European observers later claimed. In Ethiopia chronicles and religious works were written in Ge'ez; in Timbuktu, Djenné and Kano scholars such as Ahmad Baba taught law, theology, grammar and astronomy, and libraries collected tens of thousands of manuscripts. Poems, chronicles and textbooks were composed in Arabic, but also in African languages such as Hausa or Swahili written in Arabic script.

Where writing was not used, storytellers and griots preserved history in oral tradition. The epic of Sundiata, which is still performed in West Africa today, tells of the founding of Mali and is an important historical source. King lists, praise songs and proverbs carried knowledge across generations and at the same time served to legitimize rulers.

The art of the African kingdoms reached a high level. In Ife, naturalistic heads of copper alloy and terracotta were made between the 12th and 15th centuries, and in Benin guilds of casters created relief plaques and commemorative heads for the court. Earthen buildings such as the mosques of Djenné and Timbuktu, the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe and the palaces of Kilwa bear witness to sophisticated architecture.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The economy of the great empires rested on long-distance trade. After the introduction of the camel, caravans crossed the Sahara, exchanging gold, ivory and slaves from the south for salt, copper, horses, cloth and books from the north. Until the discovery of the Americas, a large share of the gold circulating in the Mediterranean world and in Europe came from West Africa.

On the east coast the monsoon trade linked the Swahili cities with Arabia, Persia, India and China. Gold from the Zimbabwe plateau reached the markets of the Indian Ocean through Sofala and Kilwa, and in return cotton textiles, glass beads and porcelain came to Africa. In the 19th century the Sultanate of Zanzibar built up clove plantations worked by enslaved people and controlled the ivory and slave trade deep into the interior of the continent.

Ironworking had been known in large parts of Africa for centuries; smiths made hoes, weapons and tools and often enjoyed special prestige. Weavers in Kano and elsewhere produced cotton cloth that was dyed with indigo and traded over long distances. Cowrie shells, gold dust, salt bars and pieces of copper served as currency in different regions.

With the Atlantic trade, commercial flows shifted to the coast. European traders supplied firearms, textiles, metal goods, spirits and cowrie shells and above all bought captives. For some coastal states this trade brought wealth and military strength, but it weakened the population and diverted the economy away from its own production. After Britain banned the slave trade in 1807, palm oil, groundnuts and ivory gained importance as exports.

title: Southeast Asia: From Funan to the Colonial Era
summary: Between India and China, trading empires, temple cities and sultanates such as Funan, Srivijaya, Angkor, Pagan, Đại Việt, Majapahit and Malacca grew up along the rivers, straits and coasts of Southeast Asia, until European companies and colonial powers had brought the whole region except Siam under their rule by 1900.
overview: Southeast Asia comprises the mainland between India and China, with the great rivers Irrawaddy, Chao Phraya, Mekong and Red River, and the island world from Sumatra to the Philippines. The monsoon winds carried ships back and forth between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea on a regular rhythm, so the region became a hub of maritime trade at an early date. From around the 1st century AD the kingdom of Funan is attested in the Mekong Delta, with its port of Óc Eo, where traders from India, China and even the Mediterranean world met. On the coast of present-day central Vietnam arose Champa, which Chinese sources mention from the late 2nd century.

Through merchants, Brahmins and monks, Indian scripts, Sanskrit, Hinduism and Buddhism reached the region; local rulers adopted them by choice and blended them with their own traditions. From the late 7th century Srivijaya, based at Palembang on Sumatra, dominated the Strait of Malacca and was a centre of Buddhist learning. On Java the Shailendra and Mataram dynasties built Borobudur and Prambanan in the 8th and 9th centuries. In 802 Jayavarman II founded the Khmer Empire, whose capital Angkor, with Angkor Wat and the Bayon, was for centuries one of the largest cities of the preindustrial world.

In what is now northern Vietnam, Ngô Quyền's victory on the Bạch Đằng River in 938 ended roughly a thousand years of Chinese rule; the later state of Đại Việt nevertheless adopted writing, Confucianism and administration from China. In Burma Anawrahta united the kingdom of Pagan from 1044, and in present-day Thailand Sukhothai emerged around 1238 and Ayutthaya in 1351. With these kingdoms Theravada Buddhism became dominant on the mainland. On Java, Majapahit rose after 1293 to become the most powerful state of the archipelago, while Islam spread along the trade routes from the late 13th century and, around 1400, the Sultanate of Malacca became the region's most important port.

In 1511 the Portuguese conquered Malacca, in 1571 the Spanish made Manila the capital of their colony in the Philippines, and in 1619 the Dutch East India Company founded Batavia on Java, from where it sought to control the spice trade. For a long time, however, the Europeans remained confined to ports and islands. On the mainland strong local states held their own: the Burmese Konbaung dynasty destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767, in Siam Rama I founded the Chakri dynasty at Bangkok in 1782, and in 1802 Gia Long united Vietnam under the Nguyễn dynasty.

In the 19th century industrialization and imperialism shifted the balance. Britain founded Singapore in 1819, conquered Burma in three wars ending in 1885 and brought the Malay sultanates under its influence. After the Java War the Dutch forced peasants to grow export crops from 1830, and in 1887 France combined Vietnam and Cambodia into French Indochina, to which Laos was added in 1893. Only Siam, under Mongkut and Chulalongkorn, remained independent as a buffer state. In the Philippines the Katipunan rose against Spain in 1896; the independence proclaimed in 1898, however, gave way to rule by the United States.
consequences: Angkor, Borobudur, Prambanan, Pagan, Mỹ Sơn and Ayutthaya are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites and have become national symbols of the states in which they lie.

The region's religious map dates from this period: Theravada Buddhism on the mainland, a Vietnam shaped by Confucianism and Buddhism, Islam in Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei, Catholicism in the Philippines and Hinduism on Bali.
The borders of today's Southeast Asian states largely follow those of the colonial empires drawn by the British, Dutch, French, Spanish and Americans in the 19th century.
The Strait of Malacca, which had already made Srivijaya and Malacca rich, is still one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world; Singapore grew from it into one of the largest ports.
Chinese, Indian and European migrants who came with trade and the colonial economy still shape the diverse societies of Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and the Philippines today.
The experience of colonial rule, forced cultivation and exploitation fuelled the independence movements of the 20th century from Vietnam to Indonesia and shapes the region's culture of remembrance.
keyFacts: From around the 1st century AD the kingdom of Funan, with its port of Óc Eo, is attested in the Mekong Delta, linking trade routes between India and China.
In 682 an inscription near Palembang records the rise of Srivijaya; around 800 the Buddhist temple mountain of Borobudur is built on Java.
In 802 Jayavarman II founds the Khmer Empire; around 1150 Angkor Wat is built, and in 1181 Jayavarman VII takes the throne and builds Angkor Thom with the Bayon.
In 938 Ngô Quyền defeats a Chinese fleet on the Bạch Đằng River, ending roughly a thousand years of Chinese rule over northern Vietnam; in 1044 Anawrahta begins his reign at Pagan.
In 1293 Majapahit is founded on Java; around 1400 Malacca emerges, and around 1431 the Khmer kings abandon Angkor.
In 1511 the Portuguese conquer Malacca, in 1571 the Spanish found Manila, and in 1619 the Dutch East India Company founds Batavia.
In 1885 Burma becomes British, in 1887 French Indochina is created, and in 1898 the Philippines proclaim independence; Siam remains the only independent country in the region.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The early states of Southeast Asia rarely had fixed borders. Historians often describe them as mandalas: around a king and his capital lay circles of princes and ports that paid tribute as long as the ruler was strong and generous, and turned to another centre when he grew weak. Power rested less on land than on people, who could be bound to the ruler, settled or carried off in war. Kingdoms such as Srivijaya, Champa or Majapahit therefore often changed their extent quickly, and their size is frequently disputed among scholars.

Kings based their rule on religious ideas from India. At Angkor the Khmer rulers linked their office with Shiva, Vishnu or the Buddha and built state temples as images of the cosmic mountain Meru; Buddhist kings on the mainland saw themselves as righteous universal rulers and patrons of the monastic order. Đại Việt, by contrast, modelled itself on the Chinese imperial court, adopted civil service examinations and law codes, and formally acknowledged Chinese overlordship in order to remain independent at home. In the sultanates of the islands the ruler's dignity combined Islam with older Malay ideas of honour and loyalty.

The Europeans brought a new kind of power: fortified trading posts, armed companies and later colonial administrations with fixed borders, maps and tax registers. For a long time the Portuguese, Spanish and Dutch relied on alliances with local princes. In the 19th century Britain, France and the Netherlands imposed their rule through wars, protectorate treaties and appointed officials. Siam kept its independence because its kings concluded treaties with all the powers, ceded outlying territories and modernized the state on European lines.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Most people lived as rice farmers in villages along rivers and on plains, as fishers on the coasts or as swidden farmers in the uplands. The basis was wet-rice cultivation, which required a great deal of shared work on dykes, canals and fields. Nobles, priests, monks, craftsmen and dancers lived at the courts and in the temple cities; inscriptions from Angkor list thousands of servants attached to individual temples. Dependants and unfree people, often debtors or prisoners of war, were numerous in almost every kingdom, because labour was scarcer than land.

In the view of many historians, women in Southeast Asia held a comparatively strong position. They worked the fields and ran markets and trade, and in many societies property was inherited through both parents. European travellers were astonished by the women traders in the ports, and there were female rulers such as the queens of Aceh in the 17th century. With the spread of Confucianism, Islam and Christianity, and under colonial law, these freedoms were restricted more tightly in many places.

The great ports were highly mixed: in Malacca, Batavia, Manila or Ayutthaya, Malays, Javanese, Chinese, Indians, Arabs, Persians, Japanese and Europeans lived side by side in their own quarters. Chinese merchants and craftsmen became an important group, but also fell victim to violence, for example in massacres in Manila in 1603 and Batavia in 1740. In the 19th century hundreds of thousands of Chinese and Indians came as labourers to the tin mines and plantations of Malaya, while forced cultivation and new taxes harshly changed peasant life on Java and in Indochina.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: From India the elites of Southeast Asia adopted Sanskrit, scripts, epics such as the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and Hinduism and Buddhism, but transformed them according to their own ideas. The result was a series of unique monuments: the Buddhist temple mountain of Borobudur, the Shiva temples of Prambanan, the temples of Mỹ Sơn in Champa, Angkor Wat and the face towers of the Bayon, and the thousands of pagodas on the plain of Pagan. The story of the Ramayana lives on to this day in dance, reliefs and shadow puppetry from Java to Thailand.

From the 11th century Theravada Buddhism from Sri Lanka prevailed on the mainland, and its monasteries also served as schools for village boys. Vietnam combined Mahayana Buddhism with Confucian learning and Chinese characters, and also developed its own script, Chữ Nôm. From the late 13th century Islam spread through the islands via traders, scholars and Sufis; Malay written in Arabic script became the language of commerce, religion and court literature. In the Philippines Spanish friars made Catholicism the religion of the majority.

In the 19th century the printing press, newspapers and schools brought new ideas. Scholars and officials in Siam and Vietnam engaged with European science, and the Siamese court itself promoted education and translation. In the Philippines José Rizal wrote novels denouncing colonial rule and the power of the religious orders, and on Java the Dutch novel Max Havelaar by Multatuli made the suffering caused by forced cultivation widely known in 1860. At the same time European scholars began to survey the old temples and decipher their inscriptions.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The monsoon winds made Southeast Asia the natural meeting point of maritime trade between the Indian Ocean and China. Ports on the straits such as Óc Eo, Palembang and Malacca thrived because ships had to wait there for the winds to change. Goods traded included Indian cotton cloth, Chinese silk and porcelain, gold, tin, fine woods, resins and above all spices: pepper from Sumatra and Java, cloves from the northern Moluccas and nutmeg from the Banda Islands, which for a long time grew nowhere else.

On the mainland wealth rested on rice. Around Angkor the Khmer built huge reservoirs, canals and embankments, although scholars disagree about their role in irrigation; aerial surveys and laser scanning have shown that Angkor was a vast, sprawling urban landscape. Đại Việt protected the Red River Delta with dykes, and Burma and Siam later exported rice in large quantities. Bronze casting, shipbuilding and pottery reached a high level of skill; ceramics from Sukhothai and Vietnam were traded as far as Japan and the Middle East.

The Europeans tried to control the spice trade by force: the Dutch East India Company imposed monopolies in the Moluccas and had spice trees outside its plantations destroyed. From 1565 the Manila galleon exchanged American silver for Chinese goods, linking Asia with the Americas. In the 19th century colonial rulers turned entire regions into export economies for coffee, sugar, tobacco, tin and later rubber; steamships, the Suez Canal from 1869, railways and telegraphs tied Southeast Asia closely to the world market.

title: The Byzantine Empire
summary: The Christian, Greek-speaking Eastern Roman Empire, with its capital at Constantinople, outlived the fall of the West by almost a thousand years, held off Persians and Arabs, preserved the heritage of antiquity and shaped the Orthodox world from Greece to Russia.
overview: On 11 May 330 Emperor Constantine the Great dedicated his new capital, Constantinople, on the site of the Greek city of Byzantium, where the Bosporus links Europe and Asia. After the death of Theodosius I in 395 the Roman Empire was divided between his sons, and the East developed increasingly along its own lines. Protected by the massive Theodosian Walls and supported by the rich provinces of Asia Minor, Syria and Egypt, it survived the migration period, while the Western Roman Empire came to an end in 476. Its inhabitants continued to call themselves Romans; the term "Byzantine Empire" was coined only by early modern scholars.

Justinian I (527–565) set out to restore the Roman Empire within its old borders. After he had brutally crushed the Nika riots in 532, his generals, above all Belisarius and Narses, conquered the Vandal kingdom in North Africa and the Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy; a coastal strip in southern Spain was added as well. At the same time he had Roman law compiled in the work later known as the Corpus Juris Civilis and built the Hagia Sophia. But the wars, a wave of plague from 541 and pressure from the Persians overstretched the empire's resources, and in 568 the Lombards invaded Italy.

In the 7th century the empire fought for its survival. After a long war Emperor Heraclius defeated the Persian Sasanians in 627/628, but following the defeat at the Yarmuk in 636 the empire lost Syria, Palestine and soon Egypt to the Arabs. Constantinople withstood several Arab attacks, thanks in part to Greek fire, and Greek replaced Latin as the language of court and administration. In the 8th and 9th centuries the Iconoclast controversy over the veneration of icons divided church and society until the veneration of images was finally restored in 843.

Under the Macedonian dynasty (867–1056) the empire revived: the missionaries Cyril and Methodius carried Christianity to the Slavs, Bulgaria and Kievan Rus adopted the Orthodox faith, and Basil II subjugated the Bulgarian Empire by 1018. The year 1054 is regarded as the moment the Eastern and Western churches split. After the defeat by the Seljuks at Manzikert in 1071 large parts of Asia Minor were lost; the emperors of the House of Komnenos stabilized the empire and asked the West for help, which contributed to the First Crusade.

In 1204 the armies of the Fourth Crusade captured and sacked Constantinople and set up a Latin Empire, while Greek successor states such as Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond emerged. Michael VIII Palaiologos recovered the capital in 1261, but the restored empire remained small, weakened by civil wars and dependent on the trading cities of Venice and Genoa. From the 14th century it lost territory piece by piece to the Ottomans until Constantinople was surrounded by only a few remaining lands. With the conquest of the city by Mehmed II in 1453 the Byzantine Empire came to an end.
consequences: The Roman law collected under Justinian was studied anew in Bologna from the 11th century and still forms a foundation of civil law in many countries of Europe and beyond.
The Orthodox churches of Greece, the Balkans, Ukraine, Russia and the Caucasus go back to the missions and church order of Byzantium; after 1453 Russia regarded Moscow as the "Third Rome".
The Cyrillic alphabet, which grew out of the mission of Cyril and Methodius, is used today for Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and many other languages.
Byzantine scholars preserved and commented on the works of Greek antiquity; with the manuscripts and teachers that reached Italy they contributed to the Renaissance.
Icons, domed churches and gold mosaics in the Byzantine tradition shape the art of the Orthodox world, and the Hagia Sophia also influenced the great mosques of the Ottomans.
The split between the Eastern and Western churches and the sack of Constantinople in 1204 still weigh on relations between Catholic and Orthodox Christians today.
keyFacts: In 330 Constantine the Great dedicates Constantinople as his new capital; in 395 the empire is divided into a western and an eastern half.
Justinian I has Roman law compiled in 529–534, dedicates the Hagia Sophia in 537 and reconquers North Africa and Italy.
In 636 the Byzantine army is defeated by the Arabs at the Yarmuk; Syria, Palestine and Egypt are lost.
In 726 or 730 the Iconoclast controversy begins under Leo III; it ends only in 843 with the final restoration of the veneration of images.
In 863 Cyril and Methodius set out on their mission to the Slavs in Great Moravia; in 1014 Basil II defeats the Bulgarians at the Kleidion pass.
In 1054 papal legates and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicate each other; in 1071 the Seljuks win at Manzikert.
In 1204 crusaders sack Constantinople; in 1261 Michael VIII Palaiologos recovers the city, which falls to the Ottomans in 1453.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: At the head of the empire stood the emperor, in Greek basileus, who saw himself as the successor of the Roman emperors and as a ruler appointed by God over the Christian world. There was no fixed rule of succession: an emperor was legitimate if he was acknowledged by the senate, the army and the people and, as a rule, crowned by the patriarch. Many emperors rose as generals or courtiers; others were overthrown, blinded or banished to monasteries. Dynasties such as the Macedonians, the Komnenoi and the Palaiologoi tried to keep the throne in the family through co-emperors and marriage alliances.

The empire was governed from Constantinople by a large administration that worked in writing and was headed by high palace dignitaries. From the 7th century the empire was divided into themes, military districts in which a commander also took on civil duties; how and when this system arose is debated among historians. Diplomacy was one of the emperors' strengths: they negotiated with gold, titles, lavish receptions and marriages, played neighbouring peoples off against each other and bound foreign princes to themselves through baptism and honorary titles.

The empire was almost constantly threatened on several fronts: in the east by Persians, Arabs and later Seljuks, in the north by Avars, Bulgarians and Rus, in the west by Normans and crusaders. Alongside the armies of the themes, mercenaries played a growing role, among them the Varangian Guard of Scandinavians and Rus. From the 11th century great aristocratic families gained power, and the emperors granted revenues from land, the pronoia, in return for military service. After 1204, and above all in the Palaiologan period, civil wars and dependence on Venice and Genoa decisively weakened the empire.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: For centuries Constantinople was one of the largest and richest cities in the world; in the 6th century it had, by estimates, several hundred thousand inhabitants. Public life took place in churches, in markets and in the Hippodrome, where chariot races were held and the people could cheer or jeer the emperor. The circus factions of the Blues and the Greens were both fan clubs and political groups. The great majority of the population, however, lived as peasants in villages, paid taxes and supplied soldiers.

Society was shaped by Christianity but was multilingual: alongside Greeks, Armenians, Syrians, Slavs, Jews and many others lived in the empire, and people from all these groups could rise in the army and administration. Churches, monasteries and endowments maintained hospitals, poorhouses and orphanages. Monasteries owned large estates and monks enjoyed great prestige; from the 10th century Mount Athos became the centre of Orthodox monasticism.

Women were legally subordinate to men but could own property and inherit, and in the upper class some wielded great power. Empresses such as Theodora, Irene, who in 797 even ruled alone as emperor, and Zoe helped shape politics, and in the 12th century Anna Komnene wrote an important work of history. Education was more widespread in the city than in the medieval West; officials, clergy and many merchants could read and write.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: Christianity was the foundation of the empire. Emperors summoned the great councils at which the doctrine of Christ was defined, for example at Chalcedon in 451; those who rejected their decisions, like many Christians in Egypt and Syria, were regarded as dissenters. Church and emperor were closely linked, but the Iconoclast controversy showed that monks and bishops could also stand up to the ruler. Over time the Greek church and the Latin church of Rome grew apart over questions such as papal primacy and the Filioque in the Creed.

Byzantine art served above all the faith. Icons, painted images of Christ, Mary and the saints, were venerated and seen as windows onto the heavenly world. Gold-ground mosaics in the Hagia Sophia, in Ravenna, in Thessaloniki or in the Chora Church in Constantinople display a solemn, otherworldly visual language. The domed church on a cross-shaped plan became the model for churches from Venice to Kyiv.

Byzantium preserved the learning of antiquity: scholars copied and commented on the works of Homer, Plato, Aristotle and the Greek physicians and mathematicians, and many ancient texts survive only in Byzantine manuscripts. Historians such as Procopius, Michael Psellos and Anna Komnene continued the classical tradition. In the 14th and 15th centuries scholars such as Manuel Chrysoloras and Bessarion brought the Greek language and Greek books to Italy and thus contributed to Renaissance humanism.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The gold coin known as the solidus, in Greek nomisma, introduced by Constantine the Great, remained stable until the 11th century and was sought after throughout the Mediterranean. Only in the 11th century was its gold content sharply reduced, until Alexios I Komnenos created a new gold coin, the hyperpyron, in 1092. The state collected taxes mainly from the rural population, levied duties on trade and used them to fund the army, administration, building projects and tribute payments to neighbours.

Constantinople lay at the crossroads of trade routes between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, Europe and Asia. Silk was especially valuable: according to Procopius, silkworms reached the empire under Justinian, and imperial workshops produced precious fabrics whose export was strictly controlled. The Book of the Eparch from the 10th century laid down how the guilds of silk merchants, goldsmiths and bakers were allowed to operate. From the 11th century Venice, and later Genoa and Pisa, received trading privileges that harmed the empire's own merchants.

In technology the Byzantines impressed with structures such as the dome of the Hagia Sophia, the Theodosian Walls and the cisterns that supplied Constantinople with water. In war they gained an advantage at sea from Greek fire, an incendiary weapon whose exact composition was kept secret and remains unknown to this day. Military manuals such as the Strategikon described tactics, siegecraft and how to deal with different enemies.

title: The European Middle Ages
summary: Between the end of Rome and the discovery of America, Christianity, feudalism, knights, monasteries, and rising cities shaped a new Europe, while the Mongols, Mali, and the Aztecs established great empires of their own.
overview: After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Germanic kingdoms arose on its soil. The most successful were the Franks: their king Clovis was baptized a Catholic around 498 and thereby won the support of the church and of the Romance population. Charlemagne extended the Frankish kingdom as far as Saxony, Italy, and Spain and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800; his reign is regarded as the birth of medieval Europe.

The High Middle Ages from the 11th to the 13th century were a period of growth. The population increased, forests were cleared, cities were founded, and cathedrals were built. Society was divided into estates: the nobility fought, the clergy prayed, the peasants worked. Through feudalism the king bound dukes and counts to himself, and they owed him loyalty and military service in return. Monasteries preserved the knowledge of antiquity, and from 1088 the first universities arose in Bologna, Paris, and Oxford.

The Crusades from 1096 brought Europe into close and often violent contact with the Islamic world, but also promoted trade and the exchange of knowledge. From 793 the Vikings from Scandinavia plundered monasteries and coasts, founded cities such as Dublin and Kiev, and reached Greenland and North America. Their descendants, the Normans, conquered England in 1066. With the Magna Carta of 1215 kings had for the first time to acknowledge the rights of their subjects in writing.

Powerful empires arose outside Europe as well: from 1206 Genghis Khan created the largest contiguous land empire in history, which allowed merchants such as Marco Polo to travel as far as China. In Mali in West Africa the gold-rich king Mansa Musa impressed the entire Islamic world on his pilgrimage in 1324, and in Mexico the Aztecs founded their capital Tenochtitlan around 1325.

The Late Middle Ages were marked by crises. From 1347 the Black Death killed about a third of the European population, the Hundred Years' War devastated France, and famines and revolts shook the established order. In 1453 the Ottomans conquered Constantinople. At the same time printing, long-distance trade, and a new interest in antiquity were already announcing the modern age.
consequences: Christianity and the church shaped the law, education, calendar, and everyday life of Europe into the modern age; monasteries and universities became centres of knowledge.
France and the Holy Roman Empire emerged from the Frankish kingdom, and many of today's European states, cities, and borders have medieval roots.
The Magna Carta and municipal charters established the idea that rulers too are bound by laws; out of this parliaments and civil rights developed.
The Crusades, the Mongol Empire, and long-distance trade connected Europe with Asia and Africa and carried knowledge, goods, and diseases such as the plague across continents.
The crises of the 14th century weakened the nobility and serfdom, strengthened the cities and wage labour, and prepared the ground for the Renaissance and the Reformation.
keyFacts: In 529 Benedict of Nursia founds the monastery of Monte Cassino; his rule shapes Western monasticism.
In 537 the emperor Justinian consecrates the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, the largest church in Christendom for almost a thousand years.
In 843 the Treaty of Verdun divides the Frankish kingdom; out of West and East Francia arise France and Germany.
In 1077 King Henry IV asks the pope for forgiveness at Canossa: the climax of the Investiture Controversy between emperor and pope.
In 1088 the first university in Europe is founded in Bologna, and around 1140 Saint-Denis becomes the first Gothic church.
From about 1200 to 1450 Great Zimbabwe flourishes in southern Africa; from 1438 Pachacuti builds up the Inca Empire in the Andes.
In 1356 the Hanseatic cities meet in Lübeck for the first Hanseatic Diet; in 1381 the great Peasants' Revolt breaks out in England.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: Medieval kings did not rule from a capital but travelled with their court from palatinate to palatinate and from monastery to monastery in order to show their presence in the land. Their power rested on feudalism: the king granted land and offices to dukes, counts, and bishops, who owed him loyalty, counsel, and military service in return and who in turn passed land on to knights. In the eastern part of the Frankish kingdom the dukes elected the king from 911 onwards, and with Otto I an imperial office arose that understood itself as the successor of Rome and of Charlemagne and that used the bishops as a support of its rule.

The dispute over who was entitled to appoint bishops led in the 11th century to the Investiture Controversy between emperor and pope, which was only partly settled by Henry IV's penitential journey to Canossa in 1077 and the Concordat of Worms in 1122. From then on the popes claimed supremacy over all rulers, called for crusades, and waged a struggle over Italy lasting decades with the Hohenstaufen such as Frederick II. In the Holy Roman Empire the princes thereby gained in independence, while in France and England the kings centralized their power.

Outside Europe empires took other paths: under Justinian the Byzantine imperial office combined Roman law, the Greek language, and the Orthodox faith; in 988, with the baptism of Vladimir, Kievan Rus adopted Christianity and writing from Byzantium. In the Andes the Inca under Pachacuti created a state that administered millions of people without writing or wheels, by means of roads, storehouses, and knotted cords. In Africa rulers such as those of Great Zimbabwe and Mali controlled the trade in gold and ivory and built their power upon it.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: About nine out of ten people lived as peasants, many of them as serfs who paid dues to the lord of the manor and performed compulsory labour. Village life followed the church year and the seasons; from the 11th century the three-field system, the heavy wheeled plough, and the horse collar for draught horses increased yields. Crop failures nevertheless led again and again to famines, and life expectancy was far below that of today. After the Black Death labour became scarce, and peasants demanded freedom and better conditions, as in England in 1381.

In the cities a new society of merchants, craftsmen, and day labourers arose, who escaped serfdom after a year according to the principle that city air makes you free. Guilds regulated the training, prices, and quality of the crafts, and the city council, usually dominated by rich merchant families, negotiated with kings and princes. Women ran workshops and shops, worked in the textile and brewing trades, and in cities such as Cologne even appeared as guilds of their own. Jews lived in separate quarters, were excluded from the crafts, and were repeatedly exposed to persecution.

The nobility lived in castles and defined itself through arms, hunting, and the tournament; the ideal of the knight combined bravery with piety and courtly manners. At courts such as that of Eleanor of Aquitaine, troubadours and minnesingers sang of love and created a poetry in the vernacular languages. Monasteries took in the sons and daughters of the nobility, cared for the sick and the poor, and offered women such as Hildegard of Bingen a space for education and influence.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The church pervaded every sphere of life: baptism, marriage, and burial, feast days, fasting, and the tithe determined the year, and the fear of hell and purgatory shaped people's thinking. The Rule of Benedict made monasteries places of prayer, work, and learning, whose scriptoria copied the texts of antiquity. In the 13th century Franciscans and Dominicans entered the cities and preached poverty, while pilgrims travelled to Santiago, Rome, and Jerusalem and relics were venerated. Byzantium and Kiev followed the Orthodox faith, which separated definitively from Rome in 1054.

With the universities of Bologna, Paris, and Oxford, a new type of place of learning arose from the 11th century onwards, in which law, theology, medicine, and the seven liberal arts were taught. Scholasticism sought to ground faith in reason; to this end Thomas Aquinas combined the philosophy of Aristotle, rediscovered through Arabic translations, with Christian doctrine. At the same time poetry flourished in the vernacular languages, from the Nibelungenlied through Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival to Dante's Divine Comedy.

Architecture reflected this new departure: the massive Romanesque churches with thick walls were followed from 1140 by the Gothic cathedrals, whose pointed arches, buttresses, and coloured glass windows let light into the interior as an image of God. Music was written down in notation for the first time, and polyphony developed in Paris. Outside Europe the builders of Great Zimbabwe raised walls metres high without mortar, and in Cusco and Machu Picchu the Inca fitted stones together so precisely that no knife blade fits between them.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: From the 11th to the 13th century the population of Europe doubled; forests were cleared, marshes drained, and settlers recruited as far as Eastern Europe. Water mills and windmills replaced manual labour in grinding, fulling, and sawing, and in the mines of the Harz and the Ore Mountains silver was extracted, which set coinage going again. Fairs in Champagne and later in Frankfurt and Geneva connected the merchants of Italy with those of Flanders and Germany.

Long-distance trade organized itself in leagues: around 1356 the Hanseatic League linked some 200 cities from London to Novgorod and traded in cloth, furs, wax, herring, and salt on its rounded cogs. Italian cities such as Venice and Genoa dominated Mediterranean trade in spices and silk from the East and developed bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping, and banks; the church forbade interest, but the merchants found ways to circumvent this prohibition. In Africa, caravans across the Sahara and harbours on the Swahili coast connected goldfields and sources of ivory with Cairo, India, and China.

Technical innovations changed everyday life and warfare: the mechanical clock, invented around 1300, divided the day into hours of equal length for the first time and struck from the towers of the cities. Papermaking, which came from China by way of the Arabs, as well as spectacles, the stirrup, and the crossbow spread, and around 1320 the first cannon appeared in Europe. In the Andes the Inca built terraced fields, suspension bridges, and a road network of more than 30,000 kilometres without iron or the wheel, on which runners carried messages and supplies.

title: The Islamic World
summary: Out of the message of Muhammad an empire arose within a century that reached from Spain to India, and whose scholars in Baghdad, Córdoba, and Cairo brought science, medicine, and philosophy to a new flowering.
overview: Around 610 Muhammad, a merchant from Mecca, began to proclaim to his fellow men revelations that, according to Islamic belief, he had received from God. His message of the one God, of social justice, and of the Last Judgement met with resistance in Mecca, so that in 622 he emigrated to Medina. There the first Muslim community arose; with this emigration, the Hijra, the Islamic calendar begins. By his death in 632 most of the tribes of Arabia had joined Islam.

Under the first caliphs, Arab armies conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Persia, and North Africa in an astonishingly short time. From 661 the Umayyads ruled from Damascus over an empire that by 711 also included Spain and parts of Central Asia; their expansion westwards was halted in 732 at Tours and Poitiers. Christians and Jews lived as protected subjects under Islamic rule; they paid a special tax but were allowed to keep their religion.

In 750 the Abbasids replaced the Umayyads and in 762 founded Baghdad, which soon became the largest city in the world. Under caliphs such as Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun, science flourished in the House of Wisdom: Greek, Persian, and Indian works were translated into Arabic, and scholars such as al-Khwarizmi, al-Razi, and Ibn Sina laid the foundations of algebra, astronomy, and medicine. The Muslims adopted the numerals with zero from India and papermaking from China.

Politically the caliphate fell apart: in Spain the Umayyads proclaimed a caliphate of their own in Córdoba in 929, in Egypt the Fatimids ruled, and Turkish sultans took power in the East. From 1096 the Crusades brought war with the Europeans; Saladin reconquered Jerusalem in 1187. In 1258 the Mongols destroyed Baghdad and put an end to the caliphate of the Abbasids.

Despite this catastrophe the Islamic world remained a connected cultural sphere in which travellers such as Ibn Battuta encountered fellow believers, mosques, and Arabic-speaking scholars everywhere from Morocco to China. Trade across the Sahara, the Indian Ocean, and the Silk Road spread Islam as far as West Africa, India, and Indonesia. Around 1300 the empire of the Ottomans arose in Anatolia, which conquered Constantinople in 1453 and became the new great power.
consequences: Islam became a world religion with almost two billion believers today and shapes the culture, law, and everyday life from Morocco to Indonesia.
Arab scholars preserved and extended the knowledge of antiquity; through translations from Toledo and Sicily, algebra, medicine, astronomy, and the philosophy of Aristotle reached Europe.
The Arabic numerals adopted from India, paper, and numerous words such as algebra, sugar, coffee, or cipher are part of the European heritage.
Muslim trade networks connected three continents and carried goods, plants such as sugar cane and oranges, and techniques such as irrigation and windmills over vast areas.
The conflicts of the Crusades and the conquest of Constantinople shaped the relationship between Europe and the Islamic world up to the present day.
keyFacts: In 624 the young Muslim community wins its first victory at Badr; in 680 the death of Husayn at Karbala deepens the separation of Sunnis and Shiites.
From 717 to 718 the great Arab siege of Constantinople fails; in 750 the Abbasid revolution overthrows the Umayyads.

Around 820 al-Khwarizmi founds algebra in Baghdad with his book on calculation; in 859 Fatima al-Fihri endows the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez, one of the oldest institutions of higher learning in the world.
In 969 the Fatimids found Cairo and in 970 the al-Azhar mosque, which still exists today as a place of learning.
In 1071 the Seljuks defeat Byzantium at Manzikert and open Anatolia to Turkish settlers.

In the 12th century Ibn Rushd expounds the works of Aristotle in Córdoba and thereby shapes the thinking of the European universities; in the 14th century Timbuktu and the Alhambra become emblems of Islamic scholarship and art.
From 1370 to 1405 Timur conquers an empire from Delhi to Ankara; in 1492 the fall of Granada ends almost 800 years of Muslim rule in Spain.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: After Muhammad's death in 632, four caliphs from his closest circle took over the leadership of the community; Muslims call them the rightly guided caliphs. Even in this period the dispute over the legitimate succession broke out: the followers of Ali, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet, regarded the leadership as a matter for his family, while the majority held the election of the most suitable man to be right. Out of this conflict the Shiites and the Sunnis emerged, and the struggles from 656 to 661 as well as the death of Husayn at Karbala in 680 became founding narratives of both branches.

The caliphs of the Umayyads and the Abbasids understood themselves as successors of the Prophet with religious and worldly authority, but in fact governed with administrations shaped by Persian practice, with viziers, tax registers, and postal routes. From the 9th century onwards provinces broke away under dynasties of their own: the Aghlabids and Fatimids in North Africa, the Samanids and Buyids in Persia, the Umayyads in Spain. The caliph in Baghdad remained a spiritual head whose name was mentioned in the Friday prayer, while Turkish military slaves and later the Seljuks exercised actual power.

From the 11th century the sultan, the holder of power in the name of the caliph, became the typical ruling figure of the Islamic world. The Seljuks, the Ayyubids of Saladin, the Mamluks in Egypt, and finally the Ottomans relied on cavalry armies, military slaves, and the revenues from land that they granted to their officers. Conquerors such as the Mongols and Timur destroyed cities and irrigation systems, but soon adopted Islam themselves and supported scholars and master builders at their courts.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The cities were the heart of the Islamic world: around the Friday mosque lay the bazaar with its lanes arranged by trade, the caravanserai for merchants, baths, fountains, and residential quarters with inner courtyards. Cairo, Baghdad, Damascus, and Córdoba were among the largest cities of their time, supplied by irrigated fields, granaries, and a network of long-distance roads. In the countryside peasants lived in villages under landlords, alongside nomads who bred camels, sheep, and horses and who protected caravans or raided them.

Religion shaped the course of the day with five prayers, the fasting month of Ramadan, the prohibition of wine and pork, and the alms tax for the poor. Christians, Jews, and Zoroastrians lived as protected subjects with their own communities, courts, and houses of worship, but had to pay a poll tax and were mostly excluded from high office; in al-Andalus and Baghdad Jewish physicians, viziers, and scholars nevertheless rose to prominence. Slavery was widespread; slaves from Africa, the Caucasus, and the steppes served in households, armies, and palaces, and military slaves such as the Mamluks could rise as far as rulership.

Women were legally disadvantaged, but received shares of inheritance, could own property, and could establish endowments. Aisha, the wife of the Prophet, transmitted hundreds of sayings of Muhammad and taught in Medina, Fatima al-Fihri endowed a mosque with a college in Fez, and rulers such as Shajar al-Durr in Egypt or Raziyya in Delhi governed in their own right for a time. In poems, travel accounts, and legal documents women appear as merchants, poets, mystics, and scholars.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: In the 8th and 9th centuries the foundations of the Islamic religious sciences were laid: scholars collected and examined the hadiths, the transmitted sayings of the Prophet, and developed four Sunni schools of law from them. Alongside legal scholarship, the mysticism of Sufism flourished, which strove for immediate experience of God; Rabia of Basra, al-Ghazali, and Rumi joined it with poetry and philosophy, and Sufi brotherhoods carried Islam to India, Anatolia, and Africa.

The translation movement of Baghdad laid the ground for centuries of original research. Al-Khwarizmi created algebra, al-Biruni calculated the radius of the earth, Ibn al-Haytham founded optics on experiments, al-Razi and Ibn Sina wrote medical textbooks, and observatories were built in Maragha and Samarkand. Philosophers such as al-Farabi and Ibn Rushd interpreted Aristotle anew; from the 13th century their Latin translations from Toledo determined the curriculum of the universities from Paris to Padua. In the 14th century Ibn Khaldun devised a theory of the rise and fall of empires that is regarded as the beginning of the social sciences.

Because pictorial representations were avoided in mosques, artists brought calligraphy, geometric ornament, and the arabesque to the highest perfection. Mosques with domes, minarets, and prayer niches, palace cities such as the Alhambra, manuscripts of the Quran, miniature painting from Persia, and carpets from Anatolia show the variety of the art. Poetry was the most esteemed art; the Persian epics of Ferdowsi, the quatrains of Omar Khayyam, and the love poetry of Hafez are still read today.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The Islamic world lay at the intersection of the trade routes of three continents. Caravans brought gold and slaves from West Africa across the Sahara to North Africa, ships sailed with the monsoon from Basra and Aden to India, East Africa, and China, and the Silk Road connected Baghdad by way of Samarkand with the Far East. A common language, Islamic law, and the gold dinar made business over thousands of kilometres easier; merchants used bills of exchange, credit, and trading companies long before these became customary in Italy.

Agriculture and technology were advanced by the farmers and engineers of the Near East: water wheels, underground channels, and cisterns irrigated fields from Persia to Spain, where rice, sugar cane, cotton, oranges, and lemons were grown. From the 8th century paper mills were established in Samarkand and Baghdad and made libraries, administration, and the book trade possible. Scholars such as al-Jazari described pumps, water clocks, and automata, and from Damascus and Toledo came famous blades, glassware, and ceramics.

The wealth of the cities depended on safe trade routes and intact irrigation systems. The devastation wrought by the Mongols in the 13th century and by Timur in the 14th, the plague from 1347, and the shift of trade to the sea routes of the Europeans from 1500 hit the old centres hard. At the same time new areas flourished: Timbuktu and Gao on the Niger, Kilwa and Zanzibar on the East African coast, Malacca in Southeast Asia, and the rising Ottoman Empire with Bursa and later Istanbul.

title: The Vikings and Northern Europe
summary: From the raid on Lindisfarne in 793 to the Kalmar Union of 1397, the peoples of Scandinavia appeared as raiders, traders and settlers between North America and Byzantium, became Christian and formed the kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden.
overview: At the end of the 8th century Denmark, Norway and Sweden were home to farming communities under chieftains and petty kings, linked to the rest of Europe by seafaring and trade. The raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793 opened the Viking Age, in which Scandinavian seafarers struck coasts and rivers from Ireland to the Mediterranean. Why the raids began just then is debated: historians point to the wealth of unprotected monasteries and trading places, power struggles at home that sent young men in search of loot and renown, possibly a shortage of land, and above all the fast, seaworthy longship.

In the 9th century isolated raids turned into campaigns and land-taking. Vikings sacked Paris in 845, founded the base of Dublin in Ireland in 841, and from 865 the Great Heathen Army conquered most of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. Only Wessex under Alfred the Great held out; eastern England was settled by Scandinavians as the Danelaw. In 911 the West Frankish king Charles the Simple ceded the area around Rouen to the leader Rollo, and Normandy grew out of it.

At the same time Scandinavians sailed across the North Atlantic. From about 870 they settled Iceland, where in 930 the Althing emerged as a common assembly. Erik the Red led settlers to Greenland around 985, and his son Leif Eriksson reached North America around 1000; the site of L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland confirms the sagas. In the east, Swedish Varangians travelled the Russian rivers as far as Byzantium and the Caliphate and contributed to the rise of Kievan Rus.

In the 10th and 11th centuries the kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden became more solid and Christian. Harald Bluetooth boasted on the Jelling runestone that he had made the Danes Christian, Olaf Tryggvason and Saint Olaf imposed Christianity in Norway, and Iceland adopted it around 1000 by decision of the Althing. Around 1028 Cnut the Great ruled England, Denmark and Norway in a North Sea Empire. When the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada fell at Stamford Bridge in 1066, the age of the great Viking expeditions ended; three weeks later the Norman William conquered England.

In the High and Late Middle Ages the Nordic kingdoms came to resemble the rest of Europe, with archbishoprics, monasteries, castles and towns. In Iceland scholars such as Snorri Sturluson wrote down sagas and the Edda, and in 1262 the island submitted to the Norwegian king. Baltic trade was dominated by the German Hanseatic League, with which Denmark went to war after taking Visby in 1361 and had to conclude the Peace of Stralsund in 1370. In 1397 Queen Margaret I united Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the Kalmar Union, which lasted until 1523.
consequences: The Vikings changed the map of Europe: Dublin, Normandy, the Danelaw in England and the settlements in Iceland and the Faroes go back to their raids and land-taking.
The Normans, descendants of the Vikings in Normandy, conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy and Sicily in the 11th century, shaping the history of western Europe and the Mediterranean.
Iceland’s Althing is regarded as one of the oldest assemblies in Europe; the names of parliaments such as the Norwegian Storting and the Danish Folketing still go back to the thing.
The Icelandic sagas, the Edda and the runestones are the most important sources on the Norse gods and continue to shape literature, music, films and games today.
L’Anse aux Meadows proves that Europeans were in America some 500 years before Columbus, even though the settlement was short-lived and had no lasting consequences.
The Kalmar Union and its break-up laid the foundations of the later states of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, whose close ties still show today in Nordic cooperation.
keyFacts: In 793 Vikings raid the monastery of Lindisfarne; in 845 they sack Paris.
In 865 the Great Heathen Army lands in England; after Alfred’s victory at Edington in 878 the Danelaw takes shape.
In 911 Rollo receives the land around Rouen, the core of Normandy, from Charles the Simple.
In 930 the Althing meets for the first time in Iceland; around 1000 the island adopts Christianity.
Around 985 Erik the Red settles Greenland; around 1000 Leif Eriksson reaches Vinland in North America.
In 1016 Cnut the Great becomes king of England; in 1066 Harald Hardrada falls at Stamford Bridge.
In 1370 the Hanseatic League secures its privileges in the Peace of Stralsund; in 1397 the Kalmar Union is formed under Margaret I.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: In the early Viking Age Scandinavia had many petty kings, jarls and chieftains whose power rested on followers, land and plunder. A leader had to bind his warriors to him with gifts, feasts and shares of the loot; whoever was successful attracted more men. Important decisions were taken at the thing, the assembly of free men, which administered justice, settled disputes and acknowledged kings. In Iceland, which had no king, the Althing became the island’s highest authority from 930.

From the 10th century royal families established themselves in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, unified the land and promoted Christianity. Harald Bluetooth had ring fortresses and bridges built in Denmark, Cnut the Great ruled England, Denmark and Norway for a time, and in Norway Olaf Haraldsson was revered after his death in 1030 as the country’s eternal king. Disputes over the throne nevertheless remained frequent, especially in Norway, where long civil wars raged in the 12th century.

In the High and Late Middle Ages the kings, with the help of the Church, expanded administration, laws and taxes and struggled with the nobility for power. Iceland and Greenland submitted to the Norwegian king between 1261 and 1264. Through marriages and inheritances the royal houses grew together, until in 1397 Margaret I united the three realms in the Kalmar Union under her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania; the union finally broke apart in 1523, when Sweden left under Gustav Vasa.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Most people in the North were farmers who grew grain, kept livestock, fished and hunted on single farmsteads or in small villages. Society was roughly divided into chieftains and nobles, free farmers who were entitled to bear arms and attend the thing, and the unfree, the thralls. Slaves were an important prize of Viking raids and were sold at markets such as Hedeby, Dublin or on the Volga. Family and honour mattered greatly; disputes were often settled by compensation payments, but could also turn into long blood feuds.

Women ran the household economy, held the keys as a sign of their status and could own property, inherit and divorce. Rich graves such as the Oseberg ship burial in Norway show the high standing of some women. How far women themselves took part in raids is debated; DNA analysis of a richly furnished warrior grave from Birka has revived the discussion. Most Scandinavians never left home, but tens of thousands emigrated to England, Ireland, Iceland or Normandy.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: Before Christianization the Scandinavians worshipped many gods such as Odin, Thor, Freyr and Freyja, made sacrifices and buried the dead with grave goods, sometimes in ships. What we know of this world of gods comes mainly from Christian sources of the 13th century, above all the Edda, and must therefore be read with caution. Writing was done in runes, whose younger row had 16 signs; thousands of runestones commemorate the dead and voyages to England or the East.

Christianization took around three centuries. After early missions such as that of Ansgar in Birka around 830, the kings converted in the 10th and 11th centuries and imposed the faith from above. In 1103 or 1104 Lund received an archbishopric of its own for the North, later followed by Nidaros (Trondheim) and Uppsala. The Church brought the Latin alphabet, monasteries and schools; in Iceland a unique literature in the vernacular arose in the 13th century, including the sagas of Icelanders and the kings’ histories of Snorri Sturluson.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The basis of their success was the longship: a slender, clinker-built boat with a keel, square sail and oars that could cross the open sea and, thanks to its shallow draught, penetrate far up rivers. Alongside it there were broader cargo ships such as the knarr, in which settlers brought livestock and supplies to Iceland and Greenland. Finds such as the Oseberg and Gokstad ships or the Skuldelev ships from Roskilde Fjord show the shipbuilding skill of the age.

The Vikings were not only raiders but also traders. Markets such as Hedeby, Birka and Kaupang linked western Europe with the East, through which furs, amber, walrus ivory and slaves were exchanged for silver, silk and wine. Tens of thousands of Arab silver coins in hoards, especially on Gotland, attest to trade with the Caliphate. Silver was often traded by weight and hacked into pieces for the purpose; in addition, English and Frankish rulers paid large tributes, the Danegeld.

In the High and Late Middle Ages the German Hanseatic League, with its cogs, took over long-distance trade in the Baltic. Visby on Gotland was an early centre, Hanseatic merchants maintained a kontor in Bergen for the stockfish trade, and the herring fishery off Scania was one of the region’s most important businesses. Dependence on Hanseatic trade led to conflicts with the Nordic kings, above all with Valdemar IV of Denmark.

title: Russia and Eastern Europe
summary: From Kievan Rus by way of the Golden Horde, the rise of Moscow and the dual commonwealth of Poland-Lithuania to the tsarist empire of the Romanovs, East Slavic, Baltic and Polish states shaped the east of Europe for more than a thousand years, until the February Revolution of 1917 brought the monarchy to an end.
overview: In the 9th century Kievan Rus took shape along the rivers between the Baltic and the Black Sea. According to the tradition of the Primary Chronicle, the Varangian Rurik was invited to Novgorod in 862; his follower Oleg made Kyiv, around 882, the centre of a loose realm of Scandinavian warriors and Slavic tribes that lived from trade with Byzantium. Princess Olga was baptized in Constantinople, her grandson Volodymyr made Orthodox Christianity the religion of the Rus in 988, and under Yaroslav the Wise Kyiv flourished with St Sophia's Cathedral and the law code known as the Russkaya Pravda. The Rus is regarded as the common root of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus.

After Yaroslav's death in 1054 the Rus broke up into rival principalities such as Vladimir-Suzdal, Galicia-Volhynia and the city republic of Novgorod. Between 1237 and 1240 the Mongols under Batu conquered most of them and destroyed Kyiv; the princes had to pay tribute to the Golden Horde on the Volga and have their rule confirmed by the khan. Novgorod was spared, and its prince Alexander Nevsky fought off the Swedes in 1240 and the Livonian Order in 1242. In the 14th century the western lands of the Rus passed to the rising Grand Duchy of Lithuania and to Poland.

Moscow, an insignificant place in the 13th century, became the seat of the metropolitan and the Horde's tax collector under Ivan I Kalita. Dmitry Donskoy defeated an army of the Horde on the field of Kulikovo in 1380, and Ivan III subdued Novgorod, ended dependence on the Tatars after the Great Stand on the Ugra in 1480 and called himself sovereign of all Rus. In the west, Poland and Lithuania joined in the Union of Krewo in 1385, defeated the Teutonic Order at Grunwald in 1410 and in 1569 merged in the Union of Lublin into the Commonwealth of the Two Nations, a nobles' state with an elected king.

Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547, conquered Kazan and Astrakhan and spread terror in his own country with the oprichnina. After his dynasty died out, famine, struggles for the throne and foreign armies plunged the realm into the Time of Troubles, until an assembly of the land elected Michael Romanov in 1613. The Cossacks of Ukraine rose against Poland-Lithuania under Bohdan Khmelnytsky in 1648 and placed themselves under the tsar in 1654. Peter the Great defeated Sweden at Poltava in 1709, founded St Petersburg and rebuilt state and army on Western models; Catherine the Great won the Crimea and, together with Prussia and Austria, partitioned Poland-Lithuania between 1772 and 1795, which vanished from the map despite the Constitution of 3 May 1791.

In the 19th century the tsarist empire stretched from Poland to the Pacific and for a time as far as Alaska. In the Decembrist revolt of 1825 officers demanded a constitution, Poland rose in vain in 1830 and 1863, and defeat in the Crimean War led to the abolition of serfdom under Alexander II in 1861. Industry and railways grew, while the state intensified the Russification of Poles, Ukrainians, Lithuanians and Belarusians and discrimination against Jews. The Revolution of 1905 forced the creation of a parliament, the Duma; in the First World War the monarchy lost its support, and in March 1917 Nicholas II abdicated.
consequences: Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians all trace their history back to Kievan Rus; who owns its legacy remains a politically contested question to this day.
Orthodox Christianity, the Cyrillic alphabet and church architecture from Byzantium shape the culture of the East Slavic countries to the present.
The experience of the partitions and uprisings made the Constitution of 3 May 1791 and the struggle for freedom pillars of Polish and Lithuanian national identity.
Expansion across Siberia to the Pacific created the largest state on earth and a multi-ethnic empire whose borders and minority questions still have effects today.
The late abolition of serfdom and rural poverty burdened Russia into the 20th century and prepared the ground for the revolutions of 1905 and 1917.
The literature, music and painting of the 19th century, from Pushkin and Shevchenko to Tolstoy and Tchaikovsky, became a lasting part of world culture.
keyFacts: In 862, according to the Primary Chronicle, the Varangian Rurik is invited to Novgorod; around 882 Oleg makes Kyiv the centre of the Rus.
In 988 Grand Prince Volodymyr is baptized; under Yaroslav the Wise (1019–1054) the Russkaya Pravda is compiled.
In 1237–1240 the Mongols conquer the Rus and destroy Kyiv; in 1380 Dmitry Donskoy wins on the field of Kulikovo.
In 1480 the Great Stand on the Ugra ends the Golden Horde's rule over Moscow; in 1547 Ivan IV is crowned tsar.
In 1569 Poland and Lithuania unite in the Union of Lublin; in 1613 an assembly of the land elects Michael Romanov tsar.
In 1648 the Cossacks rise under Khmelnytsky; in 1703 Peter the Great founds St Petersburg, and in 1709 he wins at Poltava.
In 1772–1795 Poland-Lithuania is partitioned three times; in 1861 Alexander II abolishes serfdom, and in March 1917 Nicholas II abdicates.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: Kievan Rus was not a state with fixed borders but a federation of principalities ruled by members of the Rurikid dynasty. The grand prince of Kyiv stood at the top, but succession by seniority, in which brothers and nephews moved up by age, led again and again to wars between brothers. Besides the princes, their retinue, the druzhina, and the boyars carried great weight; in Novgorod the popular assembly, the veche, even elected the mayor and the archbishop and dismissed princes.

Under the rule of the Golden Horde the Russian princes remained in office but had to pay tribute and have their position confirmed by a charter from the khan, the yarlyk. Moscow rose because its princes cooperated with the Horde, bought and married into land and drew the church to their side. Ivan III and Ivan IV turned this into autocracy: the tsar claimed unlimited power granted by God, assemblies of the land such as the Zemsky Sobor advised him only at times, and the service nobility received land in return for military service.

Poland-Lithuania was constituted quite differently. In the Commonwealth of the Two Nations the nobility, the szlachta, elected the king from 1573 onwards and bound him by contracts; the parliament, the Sejm, could be paralysed by the objection of a single deputy, the liberum veto. In Russia Peter the Great replaced the boyar duma with a Senate and specialized colleges and placed the church under a state Synod; after the partitions of Poland the tsar also ruled over millions of Poles, Lithuanians, Belarusians and Ukrainians. Only the Revolution of 1905 forced him to allow an elected Duma, whose powers he nevertheless kept narrowly limited.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The great majority of people lived as peasants in small villages of wooden houses, growing rye, oats and flax on poor soils and enduring long winters. In Russia peasants were gradually bound to the land from the late 16th century; the law code of 1649 made serfdom hereditary. Serfs could be sold, mortgaged and handed over for military service, and in the 18th century nobles often owned hundreds or thousands of them. Many villages managed land and dues jointly in the village commune, the mir.

From the 15th century peasants and adventurers fled into the wide steppes of the south and formed the Cossack communities on the Dnieper, the Don and the Yaik. They elected their own leaders, served Polish kings and tsars as border guards, but also rose in great revolts such as those under Khmelnytsky, Stenka Razin and Pugachev. Poland-Lithuania was a multi-ethnic commonwealth in which Poles, Lithuanians, Ruthenians, Germans, Armenians, Tatars and the largest Jewish community in Europe lived; the nobility made up an estimated six to ten per cent of the population, an unusually large share.

After the partitions of Poland, Jews in the tsarist empire were allowed to live only in a western Pale of Settlement, and after the assassination of Alexander II in 1881 pogroms shook the communities, whereupon millions emigrated to America. The abolition of serfdom in 1861 made the peasants personally free but burdened them with heavy redemption payments. With industrialization at the end of the 19th century, workers' suburbs grew in St Petersburg, Moscow, Łódź and the Donets Basin, where long working hours, cramped housing and strikes shaped daily life.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: With Volodymyr's baptism in 988, priests, icons, church architecture and the Cyrillic alphabet came to the Rus from Byzantium. Monasteries such as the Kyiv Monastery of the Caves became centres of learning where monks wrote chronicles such as the Primary Chronicle. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 the Muscovite church saw itself as the guardian of the true faith, and in the 16th century a monk formulated the idea of Moscow as the "Third Rome". In the 17th century the reforms of Patriarch Nikon split the church, and the Old Believers were persecuted for generations.

In the western part of the region, Catholicism and the Reformation shaped intellectual life. The University of Kraków, founded in 1364 and refounded in 1400, became a centre of scholarship where Nicolaus Copernicus also studied. Francysk Skaryna of Polotsk printed biblical books in an East Slavic literary language in Prague in 1517, and in 1596 the Union of Brest placed part of the Orthodox Church in Poland-Lithuania under the authority of the pope. Centres of learning such as the Kyiv Mohyla Academy combined Orthodox tradition with Western schooling.

Peter the Great had books printed in a simplified script and founded the Academy of Sciences in St Petersburg, where scholars such as Mikhail Lomonosov worked. In the 19th century Alexander Pushkin, Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoevsky created a literature of world rank, and composers such as Mikhail Glinka and Pyotr Tchaikovsky a musical language of their own. At the same time poets such as Adam Mickiewicz and Taras Shevchenko shaped the national consciousness of Poles, Lithuanians and Ukrainians, often against the censorship and Russification policy of the tsarist empire.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: Kievan Rus owed its wealth to trade along the waterway "from the Varangians to the Greeks" via the Dnieper and the Black Sea: furs, wax, honey and slaves went to Byzantium and the Islamic world, while silk, wine and silver came back. Novgorod traded with the Hanseatic League, which kept a trading post there, and supplied furs and wax to the west. Mongol rule destroyed many towns and crafts and burdened the land with tribute for centuries.

In the 16th and 17th centuries Poland-Lithuania became the granary of Europe: nobles had grain grown on their estates by dependent peasants and shipped down the Vistula to Gdańsk and on to the Netherlands. The tsarist empire lived from agriculture, the fur trade from Siberia and later from the iron of the Urals ironworks, which Peter the Great expanded for his fleet and army. In the 18th century Russia was one of the largest iron producers in the world, but much of the work relied on peasants assigned to it by force.

After 1861, and above all from the 1890s, Russia caught up on industrialization with foreign capital and state support under Finance Minister Sergei Witte. Coal and iron from the Donets Basin, oil from Baku and textile mills in Moscow and Łódź grew rapidly, and the Trans-Siberian Railway linked Moscow with the Pacific. Nevertheless the empire remained predominantly agrarian, and peasant yields stayed well below those in Western Europe.

title: Great Asian empires (1200–1800)
summary: From Genghis Khan's Mongol Empire to the heyday of the Qing, great empires dominated Asia: the Ming and Qing in China, the Mughals in India, the Safavids in Persia, Joseon in Korea and the Tokugawa in Japan created stable orders, magnificent capitals and economies that long outstripped Europe's.
overview: In the early 13th century Genghis Khan united the steppe peoples of Mongolia and launched a wave of conquest without parallel. His sons and grandsons subjugated northern China, Central Asia, Persia and the Russian principalities, destroyed Baghdad in 1258 and in 1241 advanced as far as Silesia and Hungary. The Mongol Empire became the largest contiguous land empire in history. After the destruction of many cities there followed a period, known as the Pax Mongolica, in which merchants, envoys and missionaries could travel under Mongol protection from Persia to China.

The world empire soon broke up into successor states: Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty in China, the Ilkhanate in Persia, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia and the Golden Horde on the Volga. In 1368 the peasant's son Zhu Yuanzhang drove the Mongols out of China and founded the Ming dynasty, which built a new capital at Beijing, sent fleets under Zheng He as far as East Africa and expanded the Great Wall into its present form. In the west, Timur built a short-lived empire around 1400 whose heirs promoted art and science in Samarkand. The Golden Horde continued to dominate the Russian principalities into the 15th century, until Moscow finally stopped paying tribute in 1480.

In India the Delhi Sultanate ruled from 1206, and in the south the Hindu empire of Vijayanagara. In 1526 Babur, a descendant of Timur, founded the Mughal Empire, which under Akbar, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb came to cover almost the entire subcontinent and produced buildings such as the Taj Mahal. In Persia, Shah Ismail I made the Shia branch of Islam the state religion from 1501; under Abbas I, Isfahan became one of the most splendid cities in the world. The Mughals and Safavids long fought over Kandahar but shared a common Persian court culture in which Persian served as the language of administration and poetry.

In East Asia long-lasting orders took shape. In Korea the Joseon dynasty ruled from 1392, and its king Sejong created an alphabet of its own. After repelling the Mongols in 1274 and 1281, Japan went through a century of civil wars until Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu unified the country. From 1639 the Tokugawa shogunate restricted contacts with the outside world and secured peace for more than two centuries. In Southeast Asia, Ayutthaya, Malacca and the Vietnamese state of Đại Việt rose, while the Khmer empire of Angkor lost its dominance.

In 1644 the Manchus took Beijing and founded the Qing dynasty, which under the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors extended its territory to Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang. At the same time Russian Cossacks and fur traders pushed across Siberia to the Pacific, so that in 1689 Russia and China agreed on a border by treaty for the first time. Around 1800 China and India were still the largest economies in the world; but the Mughal Empire was already disintegrating, the British had established themselves in Bengal, and the rejection of Macartney's British embassy in 1793 foreshadowed the conflicts of the 19th century.
consequences: For a time the Mongols linked Asia and Europe into a single space of trade and exchange; along these routes knowledge, goods and techniques such as gunpowder and paper money reached the West, but in the 14th century so did the plague.
China's present-day borders largely go back to the conquests of the Qing, and Beijing has remained the capital almost continuously since the Ming period.
The Mughal Empire and the Safavids shaped the language, architecture and religion of South Asia and Iran to this day: Urdu, the Taj Mahal and Iran's Shia character are legacies of this era.

The Korean alphabet Hangeul and the Edo culture of Japan with haiku, kabuki and woodblock prints are part of humanity's cultural heritage; Isfahan's Royal Square and the Forbidden City in Beijing are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
Russia's expansion into Siberia made it a Eurasian great power with a long border with China.
Japan's seclusion and China's self-confident rejection of European trade demands determined the course of the encounter with the West in the 19th century.
keyFacts: In 1206 Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan; in the same year the Delhi Sultanate emerges in northern India.
In 1271 Kublai Khan proclaims the Yuan dynasty; in 1274 and 1281 his fleets fail off Japan.
In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang founds the Ming dynasty; from 1405 to 1433 Zheng He's fleets sail as far as East Africa.
In 1446 King Sejong of Korea promulgates the Hangeul alphabet.
In 1501 Ismail I founds the Safavid Empire, and in 1526 Babur founds the Mughal Empire with his victory at Panipat.
In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu wins at Sekigahara; from 1639 Japan largely closes itself off from the outside world.
In 1644 the Manchus take Beijing; in 1689 Russia and China fix their border in the Treaty of Nerchinsk.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: Mongol power rested on an army organized in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand warriors, on fast mounted archers and on a network of relay stations. Conquest was carried out with great severity: cities that resisted were often destroyed completely, while those that submitted paid tribute and kept their rulers. The successor states soon adapted to the societies they had conquered: the Yuan governed China with Chinese officials, while the Ilkhans and the Golden Horde adopted Islam. The principle that only descendants of Genghis Khan could be recognized as khans remained influential into the early modern period.

The great empires of the following centuries were monarchies headed by a ruler who justified his power in religious terms.
