The Chinese emperor was regarded as the Son of Heaven holding the Mandate of Heaven, while the Great Mughal and the shah combined Islamic ideas of rule with Persian and Central Asian traditions. The Safavids relied at first on the Qizilbash, Turkmen cavalry warriors, and the Mughals on a system of ranks into which they integrated both Muslims and Hindu Rajputs. The Qing ruled as a Manchu minority through their Eight Banners while also adopting the Chinese civil service examination.

In Japan real power lay not with the emperor in Kyoto but with a supreme military commander, the shogun. After centuries of changing shogunates and the civil wars of the Sengoku period, the Tokugawa created a lasting order: some 250 lords, the daimyō, had to reside in Edo in alternate years and leave their families there. Korea under Joseon and Vietnam under the Lê dynasty adopted Chinese models of administration and formally recognized the Chinese emperor as overlord within the tribute system, yet remained independent. States such as Ayutthaya and Malacca drew their power above all from trade.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: In all the Asian empires the great majority of people lived as farmers in villages, growing rice, wheat, millet or cotton. Their taxes in money, grain or labour service paid for palaces, armies and officials. Famines, floods and wars hit them especially hard; the fall of both the Yuan and the Ming dynasties began with peasant uprisings. From the 16th century China's population grew strongly, helped by new crops from the Americas such as maize and sweet potatoes, and reached about 300 million people around 1800.

Societies were strictly hierarchical. In China the scholar-officials enjoyed the highest prestige, in Japan under the Tokugawa the samurai stood above farmers, artisans and merchants, and in Korea the yangban formed a hereditary upper class. In India castes and religious communities shaped the coexistence of Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs and Jains. At the same time great cities such as Beijing, Delhi, Isfahan and Edo – the last of which had around a million inhabitants in the 18th century – grew up with markets, theatres and teahouses.

Women usually lived under the guardianship of fathers and husbands; in China foot-binding spread, and in India noblewomen were kept in seclusion. Nevertheless, individual women wielded great influence. Sorghaghtani Beki, Kublai Khan's mother, helped steer the politics of the Mongol Empire, Nur Jahan effectively ruled the Mughal Empire alongside her husband, and court ladies, merchant women and poets in Korea and Japan left letters, diaries and poems. Shah Jahan's love for his late wife Mumtaz Mahal was turned into architecture in the Taj Mahal.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: Asia's religions continued to spread and change during this period. Through merchants and Sufis, Islam reached India, Malacca and the islands of Indonesia, while Theravada Buddhism became the dominant religion in Siam, Burma and Cambodia. In Persia the Safavids made Twelver Shiism the state religion, and in China, Korea and Japan Neo-Confucianism shaped state and family. In the Punjab the Sikh religion arose around 1500 with Guru Nanak, and Akbar had representatives of different faiths debate with one another at his court.

Scholars and rulers promoted science and learning. Ulugh Beg had an observatory built in Samarkand whose star catalogue was among the most accurate before the invention of the telescope. In Korea the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type was produced in 1377, and King Sejong had an easy-to-learn script developed as well as rain gauges and water clocks. The Ming emperors had huge encyclopedias compiled, and the Qing a collection of more than 3,000 works that also served to censor unwelcome writings.

Art and architecture reached high points. Mughal art combined Persian, Central Asian and Indian elements in miniatures and in buildings such as the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort in Delhi. Isfahan, with its great square and its mosques covered in blue tiles, became the epitome of Persian art, and the Forbidden City the epitome of Chinese palace architecture. In Japan the tea ceremony and Nō theatre developed, and later, in the cities of the Edo period, kabuki, puppet theatre, haiku poetry and the colour woodblock print.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: During these centuries Asia was the economic centre of gravity of the world. China and India produced large quantities of silk, porcelain, tea and cotton cloth that were in demand from East Africa to Europe. Under the Pax Mongolica trade on the Silk Road flourished, and the Mongol relay system linked Beijing with Tabriz and the Volga. The Yuan government issued paper money, which European travellers such as Marco Polo described with astonishment.

Maritime trade across the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea connected ports such as Calicut, Malacca, Ayutthaya, Guangzhou and Nagasaki. Muslim, Chinese, Indian and Malay merchants used the monsoon winds for regular voyages. At the beginning of the 15th century Zheng He's Ming fleets showed what technical capabilities China possessed, but afterwards the court restricted private maritime trade. From the 16th century large quantities of silver flowed from the Americas and Japan into China, where taxes were increasingly paid in silver.

Technologically, the Asian empires had mastered irrigation, canal building, porcelain making and metal casting to a high standard; the Grand Canal supplied Beijing with grain from the south. Gunpowder weapons, invented in China, became a decisive instrument of power for the Mughals, the Safavids and the Japanese lords in the form of cannon and muskets. Russian fur traders opened up Siberia for the sake of valuable sable pelts. Around 1800 the balance began to shift as European trading companies became territorial powers, above all in India.

title: The Ottoman Empire
summary: From a small principality in northwestern Anatolia grew a world empire that lasted more than six centuries and from 1453 ruled southeastern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa from Istanbul and gave many peoples and religions a common roof.
overview: Around 1300 Osman I founded one of many Turkish principalities in northwestern Anatolia, on the border with the weakened Byzantine Empire. His successors conquered Bursa in 1326, crossed into Europe in 1354 and made Edirne their second capital. With the victory at Kosovo in 1389 Serbia became a tributary, and by the end of the 14th century the Ottomans ruled large parts of the Balkans. The defeat by Timur near Ankara in 1402 plunged the young empire into a war between brothers, but it recovered within a decade.

In 1453 Mehmed II conquered Constantinople and, as Istanbul, made the city the capital of an empire that saw itself as the heir of Rome and the leading power of the Islamic world. Selim I defeated the Persian Safavids in 1514 and the Mamluks in 1516/17; with that, Syria, Egypt and the holy places of Mecca and Medina passed to the Ottomans. Under Suleiman the Magnificent the empire reached the height of its power: after the victory at Mohács in 1526 he conquered large parts of Hungary, besieged Vienna in 1529 and had administration and law reorganized.

The empire rested on a distinctive order: the sultan ruled with a grand vizier and a council, cavalrymen received the revenues of land in return for military service, and the Janissaries, recruited through the levy of boys, formed the first standing infantry in Europe. Christians and Jews lived in religious communities of their own that largely governed themselves. In the 17th century court factions, sultans' mothers such as Kösem and powerful grand viziers gained influence, and the empire held its ground despite crises until the failed siege of Vienna in 1683.

With the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 the retreat from central Europe began, and in the 18th century Russia became the most dangerous adversary; the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca in 1774 cost the empire control over the Crimea. Sultans such as Selim III and Mahmud II tried to counter the decline with reforms; Mahmud dissolved the Janissaries in 1826. The Edict of Gülhane in 1839 began the Tanzimat era, in which law, administration, schools and army were rebuilt on European models and all subjects were to be made equal before the law. In 1876 the empire received a constitution; as early as 1878, however, Sultan Abdülhamid II prorogued parliament indefinitely.

In the 19th century Greece, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria broke away from the empire, which European diplomats called the "sick man of Europe"; in 1875 the state was bankrupt. The Young Turks forced a return to the constitution in 1908, but lost almost all European territories in the Balkan Wars of 1912/13. In the First World War, fought on Germany's side, their government committed the genocide of the Armenians. After the defeat of 1918 the Allies occupied Istanbul; the national movement under Mustafa Kemal abolished the sultanate in 1922, and in 1923 the Republic of Turkey was founded.
consequences: The borders and nation states of southeastern Europe and the Middle East emerged to a great extent from the break-up of the Ottoman Empire; many conflicts from Bosnia to Palestine have their roots here.
Istanbul, Edirne, Sarajevo, Cairo and Damascus still bear the stamp of Ottoman mosques, bazaars, baths and bridges, above all the buildings of the architect Sinan.
Coffeehouses, tulips, yogurt, carpets and Janissary music travelled from the Ottoman Empire to Europe and shaped everyday life, fashion and music there.
The coexistence of Muslims, Christians and Jews in self-governing religious communities is still discussed today as an example of premodern toleration, but also of legal inequality.
The Tanzimat reforms and the constitution of 1876 were early attempts at modernization in the Islamic world, on which the Republic of Turkey and other successor states built.
The violence of the final decades, especially the Armenian Genocide and the expulsions in the Balkans, shapes the culture of remembrance in the region to the present day.
keyFacts: In 1326 Orhan conquers Bursa and makes the city the first capital of the Ottomans.
In 1389 the Ottomans win at Kosovo; in 1402 Bayezid I is defeated by the conqueror Timur near Ankara.
In 1453 Mehmed II conquers Constantinople, which as Istanbul becomes the capital of the empire.
In 1517 Selim I conquers Egypt; in 1526 Suleiman the Magnificent wins at Mohács and in 1529 besieges Vienna.
In 1571 the Ottomans lose the naval battle of Lepanto; in 1683 the second siege of Vienna fails, followed in 1699 by the Treaty of Karlowitz.
In 1826 Mahmud II dissolves the Janissaries; in 1839 the Edict of Gülhane opens the Tanzimat, followed in 1876 by the first constitution.
In 1908 the Young Turks force the restoration of the constitution; on 1 November 1922 the National Assembly in Ankara abolishes the sultanate.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: At the head of the empire stood the sultan from the House of Osman, whose rule was considered willed by God. There was no fixed rule of succession: all sons were regarded as eligible to inherit, and Mehmed II expressly permitted the victorious claimant to have his brothers killed in order to prevent civil wars. From the early 17th century the throne usually passed to the eldest male relative, and the princes lived secluded in the palace. Since Selim I the sultans also claimed the role of protectors of the holy places and later the title of caliph.

The empire was governed from the Topkapı Palace in Istanbul. The grand vizier presided over the Divan, the imperial council, in which viziers, chief judges and finance officials deliberated on war, taxes and legal cases. Many high dignitaries had entered the sultan's service as Christian children through the levy of boys and were regarded as his servants; their rise depended on merit and favour. Governors administered the provinces, and cavalrymen received land revenues, so-called timars, in return for military service.

From the late 16th century power shifted from the sultan to court factions, sultans' mothers, the Janissaries and grand viziers such as the Köprülü family, which stabilized the empire once more after 1656. After the defeats against the Habsburgs and Russia, the reforming sultans Selim III and Mahmud II began to rebuild the army and administration on European models. The Tanzimat from 1839 created ministries, new law codes and the legal equality of subjects, and the constitution of 1876 a parliament. After 1908 the Young Turk Committee of Union and Progress determined policy and led the empire into the First World War in 1914.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Ottoman society was divided into the ruling class of the askeri, meaning soldiers, officials and scholars, and the tax-paying subjects, the reaya. The great majority lived as peasants in villages in Anatolia, the Balkans and the Arab provinces, alongside nomads and a rich urban culture in Istanbul, Cairo, Aleppo, Damascus, Salonica and Sarajevo. In the cities guilds organized crafts and prices, and pious endowments maintained mosques, schools, fountains, soup kitchens and hospitals.

Christians and Jews were tolerated as protected subjects; they paid a poll tax and regulated marriage, inheritance, education and welfare themselves in their religious communities, the millets. After the expulsion from Spain in 1492, numerous Sephardic Jews found refuge in Salonica and Istanbul. At the same time non-Muslims were legally disadvantaged, and the Christian families of the Balkans had to hand over sons for the levy of boys. Slavery was widespread: prisoners of war and captives from the Caucasus, eastern Europe and Africa served in households, palaces and the army.

Under Islamic law women could own property, inherit, sue in court and establish endowments, which many women of the upper class made use of. In the palace harem, the private world of the sultan's family, women such as Hürrem and Kösem gained great political influence; the sultan's mother, the valide sultan, was one of the most powerful people at court. In the 19th century girls' schools, women's magazines and a debate about women's education and rights emerged, in which writers such as Fatma Aliye took part. Coffeehouses, bathhouses and mosque courtyards were places of sociability where news, rumours and stories were exchanged.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The Ottoman Empire understood itself as a Sunni Islamic state in which the religious law of the sharia applied alongside the laws of the sultan, the kanun. At the head of the scholars stood the şeyhülislam, who confirmed in legal opinions, the fatwas, that state measures were compatible with Islam. Madrasas trained judges, teachers and preachers, while Sufi orders such as the Mevlevi with their dervishes and the Bektashi, who were closely linked to the Janissaries, shaped popular piety.

Architecture reached its peak in the 16th century with the architect Sinan, who created domed mosques in Istanbul and Edirne that developed the model of the Hagia Sophia further. Calligraphy, book painting, tiles from Iznik, carpets and textiles are among the most important art forms. Court poetry was written in an Ottoman language full of Arabic and Persian words, while folk poets, shadow-puppet players with the figure of Karagöz and storytellers entertained ordinary audiences. Travel writers such as Evliya Çelebi and historians recorded life in the empire.

With printing in Ottoman Turkish, which İbrahim Müteferrika introduced in 1727, and the reform schools of the 19th century, exchange with European knowledge grew. Military and medical schools were founded, the first official newspaper appeared in 1831, and a press developed in which poets such as Namık Kemal spread concepts such as fatherland and freedom. At the same time national ideas spread among Greeks, Serbs, Bulgarians, Armenians and Arabs that called the common roof of the empire into question.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: In the 16th century the empire controlled the connections between the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. Silk, spices, coffee and cotton passed through Bursa, Aleppo and Cairo, and Istanbul, with several hundred thousand inhabitants, was one of the largest cities in the world. The state was concerned above all with supplying the capital and the army with grain, meat and raw materials, and it fixed prices and export bans.

Agriculture formed the basis of state revenue, which was collected first through the timar system and later through tax farming. European merchants from Venice, France, England and the Netherlands received favourable customs duties and their own jurisdiction through trade privileges, the capitulations. What had originally been a sign of the sultan's generosity became in the 19th century a gateway for European goods, against which local crafts could hardly compete.

Militarily the Ottomans led the way in the use of cannon and firearms in the 15th and 16th centuries, but later fell behind the European powers. In the 19th century the state financed reforms, railways and telegraph lines with loans from Europe, until in 1875 it had to suspend payments and in 1881 a debt administration run by creditors took over important taxes. Railway lines such as the Anatolian Railway and the Hejaz Railway, steamships and ports changed trade and travel, but also created new dependencies on foreign capital.

title: Renaissance, Discoveries, and Reformation
summary: Between 1400 and 1600, printing, humanism, the voyages to America and India, and the division of the church change Europe's view of the world and connect the continents permanently for the first time.
overview: In the 15th century scholars and artists in the Italian city-states such as Florence, Venice, and Rome turned once again to antiquity. This rebirth, the Renaissance, placed the human being and his abilities at the centre. Rich banking families such as the Medici supported painters, sculptors, and architects, and humanism spread a new form of education based on Greek and Latin sources. Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raphael created works that are still regarded today as high points of European art.

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz developed printing with movable metal type. Books thereby became cheaper and quicker to produce, and knowledge spread at a pace previously unknown. Pamphlets, Bibles in the vernacular, and scientific works now reached a broad public. Without printing neither the Reformation nor the new natural science would have advanced so rapidly.

At the same time Portuguese and Spanish seafarers sought new routes to the spices and the gold of Asia. Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, Vasco da Gama India in 1498, and between 1519 and 1522 Magellan's fleet circumnavigated the earth for the first time. Spanish conquerors under Cortés and Pizarro destroyed the empires of the Aztecs and the Inca. For the population of the Americas the arrival of the Europeans meant disease, violence, and forced labour; millions of people died, and from the 16th century Africans were carried across the Atlantic as slaves.

In 1517 the monk Martin Luther published his 95 Theses against the trade in indulgences. What began as a call for reform of the church led to the division of Western Christendom into Catholics and Protestants. Princes, cities, and peasants used the new teaching for their own ends, and Europe was plunged into wars of religion. The Catholic Church responded to the challenge with the Council of Trent and the Jesuit order.

The picture of the cosmos was also set in motion. In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus placed the sun instead of the earth at the centre of the universe, and observation and mathematics gradually took the place of the old authorities. At the end of the 16th century Europe was wealthier, better educated, and at the same time more deeply divided than ever before, and its ships connected all the inhabited continents for the first time.
consequences: Printing made knowledge available on a mass scale and created the basis for a public sphere, science, and modern education.
The voyages of discovery joined Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas into a worldwide trading network; plants, animals, diseases, and people were exchanged between the continents.
The conquest of the Americas destroyed the indigenous empires and established centuries of colonial rule as well as the transatlantic slave trade.
The Reformation divided Christendom permanently, strengthened the territorial princes, and set off wars of religion that lasted until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
The Renaissance and the heliocentric view of the world placed the human being, reason, and observation at the centre and prepared the way for the scientific revolution and the Enlightenment.
keyFacts: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invents printing with movable type in Mainz; by 1500 some 30,000 titles have been printed in Europe.
In 1492 Columbus reaches the Caribbean; in 1494 Spain and Portugal divide the non-European world between them in the Treaty of Tordesillas.
In 1517 Luther sets off the Reformation with the 95 Theses, in 1521 he refuses to recant at Worms, and in 1555 the Peace of Augsburg recognizes two confessions in the empire.
In 1543 the heliocentric world view of Copernicus and the anatomy of Vesalius appear in the same year, two cornerstones of modern natural science.
The Ottoman Empire under Suleiman, the Mughal Empire under Akbar, and the Songhai Empire in West Africa are among the most powerful states of the age.
In 1588 the Spanish Armada fails off England; in 1582 Pope Gregory XIII introduces the calendar still in use today.
Between 1500 and 1600 European traders already carry off hundreds of thousands of Africans to the Americas as slaves.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The Italian city-states were the political laboratory of the Renaissance. In Florence the Medici banking family governed from 1434 onwards without crown or title, by skilfully steering offices, elections, and patronage. Venice remained an aristocratic republic with an elected doge, Milan was ruled by dukes, and the pope was at the same time the sovereign of the Papal States. In 1513, in The Prince, Niccolò Machiavelli described soberly how power is won and maintained, and thereby founded modern political thought.

North of the Alps large monarchies grew together. Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon united Spain and completed the Reconquista in 1492 with the conquest of Granada. From 1519 their grandson Charles V united Spain, the Netherlands, Naples, Austria, and the imperial crown and ruled an empire on which the sun never set. France and England consolidated their royal power; in 1534 Henry VIII detached the English church from Rome and made himself its head.

The Reformation became a question of power. Territorial princes such as Electoral Saxony and Hesse used the new teaching to take over church property and authority over the church, and joined together in the Schmalkaldic League in 1531. After war and negotiation, the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 laid down that each territorial ruler determined the confession of his territory. In France, by contrast, the conflict led to eight wars of religion, whose climax was the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Around 1500 Europe was a society of peasants. About nine out of ten people lived in the countryside, paid dues to landlords and to the church, and in many places were serfs. The population grew again after the plague years, grain prices rose, and the Twelve Articles of the peasants of 1525 show how strongly the rural population felt threatened by new burdens. At the same time the potato, maize, the tomato, and the turkey from the Americas brought new foodstuffs to Europe in the long run.

In the cities, guilds, councils, and patrician families determined life. Craftsmen, merchants, and scholars formed a self-confident bourgeoisie that bought books, endowed schools, and had portraits of themselves painted. Women helped to run households and workshops, but were excluded from the universities and from most guilds; exceptions such as the painter Sofonisba Anguissola or the Reformation writer Argula von Grumbach remained rare. The witch trials, which increased towards the end of the 16th century, affected predominantly women.

For the peoples of the Americas and Africa the age of discoveries meant catastrophe. Smallpox, measles, and influenza, against which the indigenous population had no defences, killed the greater part of the inhabitants of Central and South America within a century. The Spanish system of the encomienda forced survivors to work in mines and on plantations. The Dominican Bartolomé de Las Casas denounced the atrocities and obtained protective laws in 1542, which however were scarcely enforced.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: Humanism was the educational movement of the age. Scholars such as Erasmus of Rotterdam sought in Greek and Latin manuscripts the unadulterated text of antiquity and of the Bible, mocked scholastic hair-splitting, and called for an educated, peaceable Christendom. Greek and Hebrew were taught at the universities, and Erasmus's Greek New Testament of 1516 became the basis for Luther's translation. Printing transformed this scholarly culture into a public debate with pamphlets, satirical prints, and songs.

In art, painters and sculptors sought the laws of nature. Brunelleschi discovered central perspective, Leonardo studied muscles and tendons on corpses, and between 1508 and 1512 Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. North of the Alps, Albrecht Dürer, Hans Holbein, and Pieter Bruegel created works that captured landscape, everyday life, and the portrait in new ways. Towards the end of the century the theatre flourished in London, and William Shakespeare wrote plays that are still performed worldwide today.

Natural research began to replace authorities with observation. In 1543 Andreas Vesalius corrected the anatomy handed down since Galen through dissections of his own, in the same year Copernicus set the earth in motion, and Tycho Brahe measured the heavens with hitherto unequalled precision. The calendar reform of 1582 showed how astronomy and the church could work together. At the same time the church defended its doctrine with the Index, the Inquisition, and the new Jesuit order, which founded schools throughout Europe and in the mission territories.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: Trading houses and banks shaped the economy. The Medici in Florence and the Fuggers in Augsburg financed popes and emperors; in 1519 Jakob Fugger paid for the election of Charles V and controlled copper and silver mining in Tyrol and Hungary. Bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping, and networks of branches made financial transactions over great distances possible. Antwerp replaced Bruges and Venice as the most important trading centre of north-western Europe.

The voyages of discovery rested on new technology. The caravel with its triangular sails could tack against the wind, the compass, the astrolabe, and the cross-staff allowed position to be determined on the open sea, and Portuguese schools of navigation collected charts and experience. Heavy ship's guns gave European fleets superiority in the Indian Ocean. Spices, silk, and porcelain from Asia, as well as sugar from the new plantations of the Atlantic islands and Brazil, became the goods of world trade.

Silver flowed from the Americas to Europe. After the discovery of the mines of Potosí in 1545 and Zacatecas in 1546, hundreds of tonnes of silver arrived each year in Seville and went on to Genoa, Antwerp, and by way of Manila as far as China. Prices in Europe rose sharply in the 16th century, which historians call the price revolution. The silver was extracted by indigenous forced labourers and African slaves, whose suffering was the other side of European wealth.

title: Latin America: colonial era and independence
summary: After 1492 Spain and Portugal built colonial empires in the Americas that rested on silver, sugar and the labour of Indigenous people and enslaved Africans; in the 19th century the colonies won their independence and, up to the Mexican Revolution, struggled over borders, constitutions and social justice.
overview: With the arrival of Columbus in 1492 a period of violent upheaval began for the inhabitants of the Americas. In the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 Spain and Portugal divided the new lands between themselves without asking the people who lived there. Spanish conquistadors conquered the Aztec Empire in 1521 and the Inca Empire from 1532; introduced epidemics such as smallpox, war and forced labour caused the Indigenous population to shrink by a large share in the 16th century. From 1500 Portugal took possession of Brazil and built up a sugar economy there.

The Spanish Crown organised its world empire into viceroyalties, first New Spain with its capital Mexico and Peru with Lima. Indigenous communities had to pay tribute and perform labour service, for example in the silver mines of Potosí, whose silver reached Seville on fleets and China on the Manila galleon. Critics such as Bartolomé de Las Casas denounced the violence and obtained the New Laws of 1542, which banned the enslavement of Indigenous people but were often circumvented in practice.

For the plantations of Brazil and the Caribbean, European traders carried millions of Africans across the Atlantic. Enslaved people resisted through flight, sabotage and revolts; in Brazil fugitives founded communities such as Palmares, which survived for almost a century. Colonial society developed a hierarchy based on origin and skin colour, headed by Spaniards and Portuguese born in Europe, followed by the American-born Creoles, mestizos, Indigenous people and the enslaved.

In the 18th century reforms by the Spanish Bourbons increased tax pressure and control; in 1780 Túpac Amaru II led the largest Indigenous uprising of the colonial era in Peru. The revolution of the enslaved in Saint-Domingue led to the independence of Haiti in 1804. When Napoleon occupied Spain in 1808, Creoles in the Americas formed governing juntas of their own; in long wars Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín and others won independence for almost all of Spain's mainland colonies by 1825, while Brazil separated from Portugal more peacefully as an empire in 1822.

The young states remained marked by border conflicts, civil wars and the power of military strongmen. After its war with the United States, Mexico lost large territories in the north in 1848, and in the Paraguayan War and the War of the Pacific neighbours fought over land and raw materials. Liberals such as Benito Juárez separated church and state, Brazil abolished slavery in 1888 as the last country in the Americas, and Cuba fought its way free of Spain by 1898. Growing export economies and mass immigration brought prosperity for elites but also new dependencies, against which the Mexican Revolution rose up in 1910.
consequences: Spanish and Portuguese became the main languages of an entire continent, and Catholicism still shapes Latin America today.

The encounter of Indigenous, European and African cultures created new societies with their own music, cuisine, religious life and art; at the same time racism and the disadvantaging of Indigenous and Black people continue to have effects in the present.
Silver from Potosí and Mexico, together with sugar, gold and later coffee, linked the Americas with Europe, Africa and Asia and contributed substantially to the emergence of a worldwide economy.
The independence movements created almost twenty independent states, whose borders largely followed the colonial administrative units.
Dependence on exporting raw materials, the unequal distribution of land and the growing influence of the United States remained central problems of the region in the 20th century.
keyFacts: In 1494 Spain and Portugal divide the non-European world between themselves in the Treaty of Tordesillas; in 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral reaches Brazil.
In 1521 the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan falls; in 1532 Pizarro captures the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca.
In 1545 the Spaniards discover the silver mountain of Potosí, the richest source of silver in the early modern period.
In 1691 Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz defends the right of women to education in Mexico.
In 1780 the uprising of Túpac Amaru II begins in Peru; in 1804 Haiti becomes independent as the first state founded by formerly enslaved people.
Between 1810 and 1825 the Spanish mainland colonies win their independence; in 1822 Brazil becomes an empire of its own.
In 1888 Brazil abolishes slavery as the last country in the Americas; in 1910 the Mexican Revolution begins.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The Spanish Crown regarded the conquered territories as kingdoms of its own, governed from Spain by the Council of the Indies. On the spot, viceroys represented the monarch: the Viceroyalty of New Spain was created in 1535 and the Viceroyalty of Peru in 1542, with New Granada and Río de la Plata added in the 18th century. Courts known as audiencias supervised the administration, and at the end of each term of office an official was held to account in a formal review. Because letters to Spain took months, colonial authorities had considerable leeway in practice, and laws from Madrid were often deferred under the principle “I obey, but I do not carry out”.

Brazil was at first granted in hereditary captaincies to private lords; because this model failed, Portugal installed a governor-general in Salvador in 1549. From the 17th century England, France and the Netherlands also set up colonies in the Caribbean whose plantations relied on slave labour. Under Spanish rule Indigenous communities kept their own local leaders, the caciques, who collected tribute and mediated between the village and the colonial state.

Independence was carried above all by Creoles, who felt passed over for offices that the Crown preferred to fill with Spaniards. After 1810 republics emerged from long wars, with constitutions modelled on the United States and France; the vote, however, mostly remained limited to men of property. Caudillos, military leaders with a personal following, frequently seized power. The conflict between Conservatives, who supported the Church and tradition, and Liberals, who demanded free trade, secularisation and civil rights, dominated the politics of the 19th century.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Colonial society was ordered by origin. At the top stood the Spaniards and Portuguese born in Europe, below them the American-born Creoles, the mestizos with European and Indigenous ancestors, the mulattos, the Indigenous population and the enslaved Africans. In practice this classification was more permeable than on paper: wealth, marriage and parish registers could help decide which group a person belonged to. Nevertheless it determined tax obligations, access to offices and education, and social standing.

The Indigenous population collapsed dramatically in the 16th century through epidemics, violence and forced labour; in central Mexico, according to estimates, by far the greater part of the people died within a century. The survivors were gathered into newly laid-out villages and had to pay tribute and perform labour service, but they preserved languages such as Nahuatl, Quechua and Maya as well as many customs. In Brazil and the Caribbean, enslaved Africans and their descendants shaped the population; they worked on sugar plantations, in mines and in households, and created spaces of their own in families, brotherhoods and fugitive communities.

In colonial society women had a subordinate legal position, but they could inherit property, run businesses and head households as widows. Convents offered women from wealthy families a place of learning, as the example of the poet Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz shows. Indigenous and African women worked as traders in markets, as domestic servants and in the fields; in the uprising of Túpac Amaru II, Micaela Bastidas took on military and organisational leadership. In the 19th century mass immigration, growing cities and the end of slavery fundamentally changed how people lived together.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The spread of Christianity was the declared aim and justification of the conquest. Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and Jesuits baptised millions of people and destroyed temples and pictorial manuscripts, but they also learned Indigenous languages, wrote grammars and recorded knowledge about the old cultures, as Bernardino de Sahagún did in his great work on the Aztecs. In popular piety Christian saints merged with older beliefs; devotion to the Virgin of Guadalupe became a symbol of Mexico, and African religions lived on in forms such as Candomblé in Brazil.

Members of religious orders argued openly about the legitimacy of the conquest. In 1511 the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos denounced the cruelty of the settlers on Hispaniola, and in 1550 Bartolomé de Las Casas defended the human dignity of the Indigenous peoples in the Valladolid debate. These debates contributed to the development of international law as formulated by scholars of the School of Salamanca.

In 1551 the first universities on the mainland were founded in Lima and Mexico, and a printing press was already working in Mexico City around 1539. Baroque churches in Mexico, Peru and Brazil combined European forms with Indigenous and African craftsmanship; in Minas Gerais the sculptor Aleijadinho created original masterpieces. In the 19th century writers searched for an identity of their own; in his essay “Our America” of 1891 José Martí called on the peoples of the continent to know themselves and their history instead of imitating Europe and the United States.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: Silver was the engine of the Spanish colonial economy. Potosí in the Andes and Zacatecas and Guanajuato in Mexico supplied most of the silver mined worldwide between the 16th and 18th centuries. From the 1550s in Mexico and the 1570s at Potosí it was extracted with the amalgamation process, in which mercury drew the silver out of the crushed ore; the poisonous mercury came mainly from Huancavelica in Peru and from Almadén in Spain. Forced labour under the mita system supplied the workers, many of whom died from accidents and poisoning.

For a long time Spain allowed trade with its colonies only through Seville and later Cádiz; as a rule, armed fleets sailed every year to Veracruz and to the coasts of Panama and Colombia. Via the Manila galleon Mexican silver reached Asia, where it was exchanged for silk and porcelain. Smuggling with the English, French and Dutch flourished nonetheless, and the colonies developed their own markets for food, textiles and livestock.

Brazil and the Caribbean became centres of sugar production: on plantations with sugar mills, enslaved people processed the cane under murderous conditions into raw sugar for Europe. Around 1700 a gold rush in Minas Gerais set off a wave of migration in Brazil. After independence the countries opened up to world trade and exported coffee, guano, nitrate, wheat, beef and rubber; railways, ports and telegraphs were mostly built with British and later also US capital. This export-oriented economy brought growth but made the countries dependent on fluctuating world market prices.

title: Absolutism and the Enlightenment
summary: Between the Thirty Years' War and the French Revolution, kings rule with a claim to absolute power, while natural science and the Enlightenment spread reason, freedom, and criticism of church and crown.
overview: The 17th century began with a catastrophe: between 1618 and 1648 the Thirty Years' War devastated large parts of Central Europe. What began as a conflict between Catholic and Protestant estates in the Holy Roman Empire became a European struggle for power, into which Denmark, Sweden, Spain, and France intervened. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the war, confirmed the equal standing of the confessions, and strengthened the territorial rulers against the emperor.

Out of the experience of war and chaos absolutism grew: the king was to rule alone and without restriction, supported by a standing army, officials, and a directed economy. Louis XIV of France, the Sun King, made Versailles the model for the courts of Europe. Peter the Great forced Russia to modernize and founded St Petersburg as a window to the West. In England, by contrast, Parliament imposed limits on royal power in the Glorious Revolution of 1688.

At the same time the new natural science changed the way people thought. Galileo, Kepler, and Isaac Newton described nature with mathematical laws; Newton's Principia of 1687 explained the motion of the planets and the fall of an apple by the same principles. Academies, specialist journals, and experiments took the place of the old authorities. These successes encouraged people to examine the state, law, and religion by reason as well.

The Enlightenment of the 18th century put everything to the test. Voltaire fought against fanaticism and censorship, Montesquieu called for the separation of powers, Rousseau devised a state based on the sovereignty of the people, and the Encyclopédie of Diderot and d'Alembert collected the knowledge of the age. Kant summed up the programme in the statement that enlightenment is man's emergence from his self-imposed immaturity. Rulers such as Frederick II of Prussia called themselves enlightened, but held fast to their absolute power.

Outside Europe, China under the Qing dynasty reached its greatest extent, while in North America English, French, and Spanish colonies grew. The Seven Years' War from 1756 to 1763 was fought out on three continents and made Great Britain the leading colonial power. On the eve of the French Revolution the Enlightenment had undermined the legitimacy of the old order, and with the steam engine a new age was already announcing itself.
consequences: The Peace of Westphalia established a European system of sovereign states that forms the basis of international relations to this day.
The absolutist state created standing armies, bodies of officials, and central administrations, out of which the modern states emerged.
The scientific revolution established experiment, observation, and mathematics as the basis of knowledge and made the technology of industrialization possible.
The ideas of the Enlightenment, such as human rights, the separation of powers, popular sovereignty, and tolerance, became the programme of the American and the French Revolution.
English parliamentary rule after 1688 became the model for constitutional monarchies and parliamentary systems throughout the world.
keyFacts: From 1618 to 1648 the Thirty Years' War devastates Central Europe; the Peace of Westphalia establishes the system of sovereign states.
In 1633 Galileo has to abjure the heliocentric world view before the Inquisition; in 1687 Newton describes gravitation mathematically.
In 1649 the English Parliament has King Charles I executed; in 1689 the Bill of Rights secures the rights of Parliament permanently.
In 1683 the second Ottoman siege of Vienna fails; Austria rises to become a great power in south-eastern Europe.
Louis XIV rules France for 72 years, makes Versailles the model for Europe, and drives out the Huguenots in 1685.
In 1748 Montesquieu calls for the separation of powers, in 1762 Rousseau devises the social contract, and in 1784 Kant defines enlightenment.
From 1639 Japan closes itself off almost completely from the outside world, while James Cook charts the Pacific between 1768 and 1779.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The absolutist state rested on three pillars: a standing army that the king maintained even in peacetime, a paid body of officials that pushed the nobility out of the administration, and a directed economy that provided the money for both. In France, Richelieu and Mazarin imposed this order against the resistance of the nobility, which Louis XIV finally bound to the court after the revolt of the Fronde. The king was held to be appointed by God, and Bishop Bossuet taught that no one might demand an account from him. In practice provincial estates, parlements, and privileges continued to exist, and royal power was never as unrestricted as the theory claimed.

England took a different path. The conflict between king and Parliament over taxes and religion led in 1642 to the civil war, which ended with the execution of Charles I and the republic under Oliver Cromwell. After the return of the monarchy in 1660 and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 it was clear that the king could govern only with Parliament. John Locke supplied the justification: governments exist to protect life, liberty, and property, and may be deposed if they violate this task.

In the 18th century the European system of powers was determined by five great powers: France, Great Britain, Austria, Prussia, and Russia. Wars such as the War of the Spanish Succession, the War of the Austrian Succession, and the Seven Years' War turned on the balance of power, claims of inheritance, and colonies. Rulers such as Frederick II, Maria Theresa, Joseph II, and Catherine II called themselves enlightened and reformed schools, justice, and administration, but in 1772 jointly partitioned Poland and held fast to their unlimited power.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Society was divided into estates: the clergy and the nobility enjoyed exemption from taxes and privileges of honour, while the Third Estate, that is peasants, craftsmen, merchants, and scholars, bore the burdens. The Thirty Years' War had depopulated Germany, and only around 1700 was the level of 1618 reached again. Famines, infant mortality, and epidemics determined everyday life; the plague raged in London in 1665 and in Marseille in 1720. The witch trials, which reached their peak between 1560 and 1630, claimed tens of thousands of victims in Europe, predominantly women.

At the same time a new public sphere emerged. In coffee houses, reading societies, salons, and Masonic lodges, townspeople and nobles discussed politics, science, and literature. Newspapers and journals such as the English Spectator reached a growing readership, and the number of people able to read rose. Women such as the Marquise du Deffand or Madame Geoffrin ran salons in Paris where the thinkers of the Enlightenment met, and scholars such as Émilie du Châtelet or the astronomer Maria Winkelmann carried out research despite all obstacles.

At court, ceremonial governed every step. The king's rising and dressing was a public act at Versailles, in which the order of those present showed their rank. Wigs, hooped skirts, chocolate, and coffee spread from the court into the cities. For the majority of people in the countryside, however, little changed; in Eastern Europe serfdom even grew harsher, and in Russia landowners could sell their peasants like cattle.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The scientific revolution changed the relationship of human beings to the world. In 1609 Galileo turned the telescope on the heavens, Kepler found the laws of the planetary orbits, William Harvey discovered the circulation of the blood, and Newton brought heaven and earth together under a single law. Academies such as the Royal Society in London and the Académie des sciences in Paris organized the exchange of observations, experiments, and criticism. The microscope, the telescope, the air pump, and the pendulum clock extended the senses and made measurement the basis of knowledge.

The Enlightenment transferred this confidence in reason to society, law, and religion. Pierre Bayle and Voltaire demanded tolerance, Montesquieu examined the laws and constitutions of peoples, Rousseau asked after a just order, and Beccaria called for the abolition of torture and the death penalty. Deism saw in God a clockmaker who had created the world and no longer intervened in it; others remained devout but demanded a reasonable religion without superstition. In Germany, Lessing, Mendelssohn, and Kant combined the Enlightenment with religious tolerance and ethics.

Art and music flourished with the Baroque and the Rococo. Magnificent palaces, churches and gardens such as those at Versailles, Würzburg and Schönbrunn were meant to display the power of princes and church. Johann Sebastian Bach, George Frideric Handel and later Haydn and Mozart created works that belong to the core of European music. The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 shook the belief in a best of all possible worlds and set off a debate about God, nature and evil that Voltaire took up in his Candide.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: Mercantilism was the economic doctrine of absolutism. According to Colbert's ideas, a state should export more than it imported in order to keep gold and silver in the country. Manufactories for luxury goods such as tapestries, mirrors and porcelain were founded, tariffs protected domestic production, and colonies supplied raw materials and bought finished goods. In Prussia and Austria the doctrine was called cameralism and served above all to fill the prince's coffers for the army and the administration.

The Netherlands and England developed a different form of economic activity. Trading companies such as the Dutch and the English East India Company were joint-stock companies with their own fleets, fortresses and soldiers; the Amsterdam stock exchange and the Bank of England, founded in 1694, became centers of capital. The triangular trade between Europe, Africa and the Americas in goods, slaves and plantation products such as sugar, tobacco and coffee brought enormous profits. In 1776 Adam Smith criticized mercantilism and called for free trade as the source of prosperity.

In agriculture, the agricultural revolution began in England with new crop rotations, the cultivation of clover, animal breeding and the enclosure of common land. The potato prevailed against resistance in Prussia and other countries and reduced famines. From 1712 onward, steam engines of Newcomen's design pumped water out of mines, and the improvement by James Watt from 1769 as well as mechanical spinning machines announced industrialization. Canals, paved roads and stagecoaches sped up traffic within Europe.

title: Age of Revolutions
summary: From American independence through the French Revolution and Napoleon to the Revolution of 1848: human rights, nation and popular sovereignty overthrow the old order.
overview: In 1776 thirteen British colonies in North America declared their independence, invoking the Enlightenment: all men are created equal and have a right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Under George Washington and with French help they won the war against the mother country. The Constitution of 1787 created the first modern republic with a separation of powers and an elected president.

France had overstretched itself financially by supporting the Americans. When King Louis XVI convened the Estates General in 1789, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly, and on 14 July the people of Paris stormed the Bastille. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, the abolition of noble privileges and a constitution followed. The attempt to preserve the monarchy failed; in 1792 the republic was proclaimed and in 1793 the king was executed.

Threatened by enemies abroad and uprisings at home, the Jacobins under Robespierre established a reign of terror to which thousands of people fell victim on the guillotine. In the colony of Saint-Domingue, too, the enslaved rose up in 1791; under Toussaint Louverture they won the abolition of slavery, and in 1804 Haiti came into being as the first state founded by former slaves. Olympe de Gouges demanded equal rights for women and was executed for it.

Out of the revolutionary wars rose the general Napoleon Bonaparte, who seized power in a coup in 1799 and crowned himself emperor in 1804. He reorganized France with the Code civil, defeated Austria, Prussia and Russia and dominated almost all of Europe. The campaign into Russia in 1812 ended in catastrophe; the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig in 1813 and Waterloo in 1815 ended his rule. The Congress of Vienna restored the monarchies and sought to suppress revolutionary ideas.

Yet the ideas of liberty, nation and constitution could no longer be pushed back. In Latin America, Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led the Spanish colonies to independence, Greece broke away from the Ottoman Empire, and in 1830 Paris once again overthrew its king. In 1848 a wave of revolution swept across almost all of Europe; in Frankfurt the first all-German national assembly convened. The revolution failed, but its demands for basic rights and national unity remained on the agenda.
consequences: The human and civil rights of 1776 and 1789 became the benchmark for constitutions and basic rights throughout the world.
The idea of popular sovereignty replaced the divine right of kings as the basis of political rule and initiated the transition to constitutional states and democracies.
The Code civil spread equality before the law, freedom of property and the separation of state and church across Europe and shaped numerous legal systems.
The revolutions in Haiti and Latin America largely ended European colonial rule on the American continent and set an example against slavery.
Nationalism and liberalism became the defining political forces of the 19th century and led to new nation-states such as Italy and Germany.
keyFacts: In 1787 the United States gives itself the first modern written constitution with a separation of powers in Philadelphia; in 1791 the basic rights of the Bill of Rights follow.
In October 1789 the march of thousands of Parisian women to Versailles forces the king to move to Paris; in 1794 the National Convention abolishes slavery in the French colonies.
From 1798 to 1801 Napoleon's campaign to Egypt fails militarily but establishes modern Egyptology; in 1804 Haiti becomes independent as the first state founded by former slaves.
In 1806 Francis II lays down the crown of the Holy Roman Empire; from 1807 onward the Prussian Reforms modernize the state, the army and education.
In 1812 Napoleon loses the greater part of his army in Russia; in 1815 his rule ends for good at Waterloo.
From 1810 to 1821 Mexico wins its independence from Spain; in 1830 the July Revolution in Paris overthrows the Bourbons.
In 1832 around 30,000 people at the Hambach Festival demand freedom and German unity; the colors black, red and gold become the symbol of the movement.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The revolutions in America and France gave a new answer to the same question: where does the power of the state come from? In place of the king by the grace of God came the people as the bearer of sovereignty, giving themselves a constitution through elected representatives. The American Constitution of 1787 put Montesquieu's separation of powers into practice with Congress, president and Supreme Court; within ten years France tried out a constitutional monarchy, a radical republic, the dictatorship of the Committee of Public Safety and the Directory before Napoleon seized power.

Napoleon ruled as emperor with plebiscites, a compliant parliament and a tightly organized administration, but with his conquests he exported the law code, equality before the law and the dissolution of the old imperial structures to half of Europe. The reforms in Prussia, Bavaria and Austria were in part responses to this challenge: states that wanted to survive had to turn their subjects into citizens who were willing to fight for the fatherland and to pay taxes.

After 1815 the monarchs under Metternich's leadership tried to turn back the clock. Censorship, police informers, the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 and the interventions of the Holy Alliance in Spain and Italy were meant to stifle constitutions and national movements. But Great Britain withdrew from the system, Greece, Belgium and the Latin American states won their independence, and the July Revolution of 1830 showed that kings who broke the constitution could be overthrown. The Vormärz, the period between 1815 and 1848, was a race between repression and a growing desire for freedom.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The revolution put an end to the society of estates. Noble titles, tithes, compulsory labor services and guild constraints were abolished in France between 1789 and 1791, church property was auctioned off and peasants became owners of their land. The new masters were the propertied middle class, lawyers, merchants and officials; the artisans and small traders of the cities, the sansculottes, had driven the revolution forward in the streets but mostly remained excluded from the vote. In Prussia the October Edict of 1807 abolished the hereditary subjection of the peasants, yet many lost their land to the manorial lords when redeeming their obligations.

Women helped carry the revolution, from the march on Versailles through the political clubs to the women who followed Napoleon to war as sutlers. Olympe de Gouges in France and Mary Wollstonecraft in England demanded equal rights, yet in 1793 the revolution excluded women from politics, and the Code civil placed them under the guardianship of men. Slavery was abolished in the French colonies in 1794, reintroduced by Napoleon in 1802 and eliminated in Haiti by the enslaved themselves; in the United States the constitution entrenched slavery, and in 1807 Britain at first banned only the slave trade.

War shaped the everyday life of an entire generation. General conscription, introduced in France in 1793, sent millions of young men into the armies; billeting, requisitions, epidemics and the British naval blockade struck the civilian population. At the same time a political public sphere emerged with newspapers, pamphlets, songs and festivals such as the Hambach Festival, and colors, cockades and anthems such as the Marseillaise made politics a matter of feeling.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The revolution intervened deeply in religion. In 1789 France nationalized church property, made priests swear an oath to the constitution and in 1793 attempted to replace Christianity with a cult of reason and a new calendar; in the Concordat of 1801 Napoleon reconciled with the pope but kept the church under state supervision. In Germany the Imperial Recess of 1803 dissolved the ecclesiastical principalities and monasteries, and Jews received civil rights for the first time in France in 1791 and in Prussia in 1812.

Art became political. Jacques-Louis David painted the Tennis Court Oath and the murdered Marat, Goya recorded the execution of the Madrid insurgents in 1808, and in 1830 Delacroix created Liberty Leading the People. Beethoven struck out the dedication of his Third Symphony to Napoleon when the latter crowned himself emperor; poets such as Byron and Hölderlin were enthusiastic about the freedom of Greece. Romanticism discovered folk songs, fairy tales and the medieval past and thereby contributed to the emergence of national identities.

Science and education became tasks of the state. France introduced the metric system, the Polytechnic School and a centrally directed school system; the scholars who accompanied Napoleon to Egypt founded Egyptology with the Description de l'Égypte and the Rosetta Stone. In 1810 Wilhelm von Humboldt founded the University of Berlin on the principle of the unity of research and teaching, and the Brothers Grimm, linguists and historians, made the universities carriers of the national idea.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The revolution created the legal foundations of the market economy: freedom of trade, the abolition of the guilds, protection of property, uniform weights and measures and, in France in 1800, the Bank of France. The Code civil and the Prussian Reforms made it possible to buy and sell land freely and to practice any trade. The customs barriers between hundreds of small German states fell only gradually; the German Customs Union of 1834 was a late fruit of this development.

Napoleon's Continental Blockade against British goods from 1806 was intended to bring Great Britain economically to its knees, but above all it encouraged smuggling and drove up the prices of sugar and coffee; at the same time it stimulated the cultivation of sugar beet and the textile industry on the continent. Great Britain, protected by its fleet, financed the coalitions against France with the profits of its incipient industrialization and emerged from the wars as the leading economic power.

The technology of war and of the state changed. Mass armies needed standardized rifles, tin cans, which Napoleon's government brought forth through a prize competition, and the optical telegraph, which carried messages from Paris to the frontiers within hours. After 1815 the steam engine and the railroad reached the continent; the first German railway ran from Nuremberg to Fürth in 1835, and the labor question, which came onto the agenda in 1848, was already making itself felt in the textile towns.

title: Industrialization, Nation-States and Imperialism
summary: The steam engine, the factory and the railroad change work and everyday life, new nation-states emerge, and the European powers divide the world into colonies.
overview: From the late 18th century onward, an upheaval began in England that is known as the Industrial Revolution. The steam engine improved by James Watt powered spinning machines, looms, pumps and soon locomotives as well. Work shifted from workshops and farms into factories, and coal and iron became the raw materials of the new age. Cities such as Manchester, Birmingham and later the Ruhr region grew many times over within a few decades.

Industrialization created enormous wealth, but also new social questions. Factory workers, among them many women and children, worked twelve hours a day and more, lived in cramped tenements and had hardly any rights. Out of this experience arose trade unions, cooperatives and political parties. In the Communist Manifesto of 1848, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels interpreted history as a struggle between classes and called for a society without private ownership of the means of production.

At the same time the nation-state became the guiding model of politics. In Europe, new large states emerged with Italy in 1861 and the German Empire in 1871; in the United States the Civil War from 1861 to 1865 secured the unity of the Union and ended slavery. After the Meiji Restoration of 1868, Japan deliberately opened itself to Western technology and administration and rose within a single generation to become an industrial and military power.

With economic and military superiority grew the claim of the industrial states to colonies, raw materials and markets. Great Britain forced China to open up in the Opium War, the Suez Canal shortened the route to India, and at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 the European powers laid down rules for the partition of Africa. The resistance of the colonized was often brutally broken, for example in the genocide of the Herero and Nama in German South West Africa.

Around 1900 technical progress seemed boundless: electricity, the telephone, the automobile, the airplane and Marie Curie's discoveries in physics shaped the sense of life. At the same time the great powers armed, concluded alliances and competed over fleets and colonies. These tensions erupted in 1914 in the First World War.
consequences: The factory, the machine and fossil energy have shaped the economy and everyday life ever since; today's economic growth as well as climate change have their roots here.
Out of the social question arose the labor movement, social legislation and the political ideas of socialism and communism, which determined the 20th century.
Nation-states such as Germany, Italy, the United States and Japan became the decisive actors in world politics.
The colonial partition of Africa and Asia left behind arbitrary borders, economic dependencies and conflicts whose effects are still felt today.
The rivalry of the imperialist great powers led directly into the First World War.
keyFacts: From about 1780 onward, a completely new form of economic activity emerges in England with the steam engine, the mechanical loom and the factory.
In 1833 the British Empire abolishes slavery, in 1861 Russia abolishes serfdom, and in 1865 slavery ends in the United States.
In 1859 Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species shakes the worldview of many people.
In 1863 the Red Cross is founded in Geneva, and in 1864 the first Geneva Convention follows.
From 1883 to 1889 Bismarck introduces the world's first state social insurance schemes.
In 1893 New Zealand becomes the first country in the world in which women receive the vote at the national level.
Around 1900 the European powers, the United States and Japan control almost the entire earth as colonies or spheres of influence.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The 19th century was the age of constitutions and parliaments, but not of democracy in today's sense. In Great Britain the electoral reforms of 1832, 1867 and 1884 gradually widened the circle of voters, while in Prussia the three-class franchise based on tax payments determined the weight of a vote until 1918. Women remained excluded almost everywhere; only New Zealand granted them the vote in 1893, followed by Australia in 1902 and Finland in 1906. Monarchs such as William I, Franz Joseph and Tsar Alexander II ruled with ministers and officials who were increasingly selected according to merit rather than origin.

The nation-state became the dominant political idea. Italy united between 1859 and 1870 under Cavour and Garibaldi, and Germany in 1871 under Prussian leadership. In the multiethnic empires of the Habsburgs, Ottomans and Romanovs, Czechs, Hungarians, Poles, Serbs and other peoples demanded rights of their own or states of their own. Nationalism combined with compulsory schooling, conscription, monuments and national holidays to form a mass movement that placed loyalty to the state above all other ties.

Abroad, the great powers pursued imperialism. Great Britain ruled over a quarter of the earth, France built an empire in North Africa and Indochina, Russia expanded into Central Asia, and in 1898 the United States took the Philippines and Puerto Rico from Spain. Japan's victory over Russia in 1905 showed for the first time that an Asian power could defeat a European great power. Alliances such as the Dual Alliance of 1879 and the Entente cordiale of 1904 divided Europe into two camps that collided in 1914.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The population of Europe doubled in the 19th century, and millions of people moved from the countryside into the cities. Berlin grew from 170,000 inhabitants in 1800 to over two million in 1910. In the working-class districts, families shared one or two rooms with lodgers and night sleepers, water came from the courtyard, and sewage ran in open gutters. Cholera, which reached Europe from India in 1831, killed tens of thousands in such districts until sewer systems, waterworks and the discoveries of Robert Koch and Louis Pasteur pushed back the epidemics.

The world of work determined life. Around 1850 a factory worker worked twelve to fourteen hours on six days a week, and children from the age of eight or nine stood at the spinning machines because they were small enough to crawl under them. The first laws, such as the Prussian regulation of 1839 or the British Factory Act of 1833, restricted child labor but were hardly enforced. From famines such as the Irish one of 1845 and from the Silesian weavers' uprising of 1844, contemporaries learned that hardship could become political.

Toward the end of the century, living conditions improved noticeably. Wages rose, working hours fell to ten, and trade unions and social insurance offered protection in sickness and old age. Department stores, sports clubs, bicycles, cinemas and summer holidays at the seaside were part of a new leisure culture. Millions of Europeans, above all from Ireland, Italy, Germany and Eastern Europe, emigrated to America; between 1880 and 1914 alone, over 20 million people left the continent.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The natural sciences experienced their greatest flowering. Darwin's theory of evolution of 1859, the bacteriology of Koch and Pasteur, the electrodynamics of Faraday and Maxwell, the discovery of X-rays in 1895 and of radioactivity by Becquerel and the Curies changed the picture of nature and of humanity. Universities and research laboratories, above all the German ones, became engines of progress; the chemical industry developed synthetic dyes, fertilizers and medicines such as aspirin in 1899.

Religion and the churches came under pressure but remained powerful. In Germany, Bismarck fought the influence of the Catholic Church in the Kulturkampf of the 1870s, and in France church and state were separated in 1905. At the same time missionary societies arose that went to Africa and Asia with the colonial powers, as did religious reform movements such as the Salvation Army, which took up the cause of the poor in the industrial cities. With the Red Cross and Bertha von Suttner's peace movement, new nondenominational forms of humanitarian commitment emerged.

Art and literature reflected the upheavals. The realism of Dickens, Zola and Fontane described life in factories and tenements, and the Impressionists around Monet painted railway stations, boulevards and the light of the big city. The mass press, lending libraries and compulsory schooling caused the number of readers to explode. The world's fairs from London in 1851 to Paris in 1900 with the Eiffel Tower of 1889 staged technology and colonies as a spectacle for millions of visitors.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The first industrialization rested on coal, iron and textiles. James Hargreaves's spinning jenny from the 1760s and Edmund Cartwright's mechanical loom of 1785 multiplied the production of yarn and cloth, and the puddling process and later the Bessemer process of 1856 made steel cheap. The railway network in Germany grew from six kilometers in 1835 to over 60,000 kilometers in 1910. Canals, steamships and, from 1869, the Suez Canal connected the markets of the world.

From about 1870 the second Industrial Revolution began with electricity, chemistry and the internal combustion engine. Werner von Siemens developed the dynamo in 1866, Thomas Edison a usable light bulb in 1879 and the first power station in 1882, and Carl Benz the automobile in 1886. New large enterprises such as Krupp, Siemens, Bayer, Standard Oil and US Steel employed tens of thousands of workers and formed cartels and trusts. From 1866 the telegraph connected Europe and America permanently, and Alexander Graham Bell's telephone of 1876 followed.

The world economy became a single market. Grain from North America and Russia, wool from Australia, rubber from the Congo and cotton from India and Egypt flowed into the industrial countries, which in return exported machines, textiles and capital. The gold standard secured fixed exchange rates, and London was the financial center of the world. This interconnection brought prosperity, but also crises such as the crash of 1873, and it often rested on the exploitation of colonies and plantation workers.

title: First World War and Interwar Period
summary: The First World War destroys the old order of Europe; revolutions, fragile peace treaties and the Great Depression shape the turbulent years up to 1939.
overview: In the summer of 1914, the assassination of the Austrian heir to the throne in Sarajevo set off a chain of alliance obligations and mobilizations. Within a few weeks the Central Powers of Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire faced the Entente of France, Russia and Great Britain. The short war that had been expected congealed in the west into a war of position in which machine guns, artillery and poison gas killed hundreds of thousands without the front moving appreciably.

The war became the first total war in history: entire national economies were converted to armaments, women took over the work of men in factories, and the civilian population suffered from blockade and hunger. In 1917 the balance tipped: Russia plunged into revolution and withdrew from the war, while the United States entered on the side of the Entente. In November 1918 the Central Powers collapsed, Emperor William II abdicated, and the Armistice of Compiègne ended the fighting.

The Paris suburb treaties of 1919 and 1920 reordered Europe and the Middle East. The empires of the Habsburgs, Romanovs, Hohenzollerns and Ottomans had disappeared; in their place came new nation-states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and Turkey. The Treaty of Versailles imposed war guilt, territorial cessions and high reparations on Germany, which many Germans felt to be a humiliation. The League of Nations was meant to prevent future wars, but remained weak without the United States and without means of power of its own.

In Russia the Bolsheviks under Lenin established the Soviet Union, the first communist state, after civil war and terror. In Italy, Mussolini came to power with the Fascists in 1922; in Germany the Weimar Republic foundered on inflation, political violence and the Great Depression until Hitler took power in 1933. The crisis of 1929 caused unemployment to explode worldwide and strengthened radical forces everywhere.

The 1930s were marked by rearmament and aggression. Japan occupied Manchuria, Italy attacked Ethiopia, and in the Spanish Civil War from 1936 to 1939 Germany and Italy tested their weapons at Franco's side while the democracies looked on. When Germany attacked Poland in September 1939, the next world war could no longer be prevented.
consequences: Around 17 million dead, devastated landscapes and a traumatized generation shaped Europe; the war is regarded as the primal catastrophe of the 20th century.
Four empires disappeared, and the map of Europe and the Middle East was redrawn; many border conflicts up to the present day go back to this.
With the Soviet Union, the first communist state came into being, and it determined world politics until 1991.
Defeat in the war, the Treaty of Versailles and the Great Depression created the conditions for the rise of fascism and National Socialism.
The League of Nations failed, but it provided the model for the United Nations after 1945.
keyFacts: In September 1914 the Battle of the Marne halts the German advance; by the end of the year the western front from the North Sea to the Swiss border has congealed into trench warfare.
In 1915 the genocide of the Armenians begins in the Ottoman Empire, claiming an estimated one million victims by 1916; in the same year the Allied landing at Gallipoli fails.
On 9 November 1918 the republic is proclaimed in Berlin; on 12 November women in Germany receive the vote and go to the polls for the first time on 19 January 1919.
Between 1918 and 1920 the Spanish flu kills at least 20 to 50 million people worldwide, more than the war itself.
On 11 August 1919 the Weimar Constitution comes into force; in the same year Walter Gropius founds the Bauhaus in Weimar.
In 1923 Germany experiences the occupation of the Ruhr, hyperinflation and Hitler's putsch; the Rentenmark and the Locarno Treaties of 1925 usher in a brief phase of stability.

In 1930 Gandhi leads the Salt March against British rule in India, in 1934/35 Mao's Red Army saves itself in the Long March, and from 1936 to 1938 Stalin has hundreds of thousands murdered in the Great Purge.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: During the war, power shifted in all states toward the military and the governments. In Germany, from 1916 onward the Supreme Army Command under Hindenburg and Ludendorff effectively governed, stripping the emperor of power, pushing through unrestricted submarine warfare and, in the autumn of 1918, shifting responsibility for the armistice onto the parties of the Reichstag. The political truce between the parties proclaimed at the start of the war broke apart in 1917 over the question of war aims, when the Reichstag passed a peace resolution without annexations. In France and Great Britain too, determined wartime premiers took the helm in Clemenceau and Lloyd George, the press was censored, and opponents of the war were persecuted.

With proportional representation, referendums and a directly elected Reich president, the Weimar Republic created one of the most modern constitutions of its time, yet Article 48 allowed the president to govern past parliament by emergency decree. The republic was fought from the right and from the left: the Kapp Putsch of 1920 failed only because of the workers' general strike, and the political murders of Matthias Erzberger in 1921 and Walther Rathenau in 1922 showed the readiness for violence of right-wing secret societies. From 1930 presidential cabinets governed by emergency decree, and the parties of the center lost ground to the National Socialists and the Communists.

Outside Germany, new movements shaped politics. In Italy, Mussolini forced his appointment as head of government with the March on Rome in 1922 and built up the first fascist state by 1926. In the Soviet Union, Stalin prevailed after Lenin's death against Trotsky, whom he expelled from the country in 1929, and established sole rule with a secret police and camps. The British Empire came under pressure: in Ireland the Easter Rising of 1916 led by way of a war of independence to the Irish Free State of 1922, and in India the Amritsar massacre of 1919 turned Gandhi's movement of nonviolence into a mass movement.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The war changed the life of the civilian population profoundly. Millions of women worked in munitions factories, as streetcar conductors, in offices and military hospitals, and kept agriculture running; in Germany the number of women workers in the armaments industry rose to over two million. In the turnip winter of 1916/17, the British naval blockade led to hunger in German cities, from whose effects hundreds of thousands died. At the front, by contrast, the Christmas truce of 1914, when German and British soldiers in Flanders sang together, exchanged gifts and played football, showed how alien the hatred of propaganda could be to ordinary soldiers; in the following years the army commands strictly forbade such fraternization.

After the war, in Germany alone there lived around 2.7 million war-disabled, along with hundreds of thousands of widows and orphans whose support burdened state budgets.
